entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams: Having my character questioned was 'added motivation'
entries.summary: <p>Caleb Williams heard the jokes about his toughness after he was carted off the field in Week 2 with an injury that would keep him out for three games. That was clear last week when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears quarterback</a> laid out his complaints about the reporting surrounding his hamstring injury.</p><p></p><p>It was also an insight into what slights — real or perceived — fueled him during three weeks of rehab.</p><p></p><p>“A little bit, a little bit,” he said Tuesday after the team’s walk-through. “I think that’s more of the <i>added</i> motivation. The motivation is just being able to try to get back out there with my guys, us losing the week before, all of those things.</p><p></p><p>“And then being able to have people question me and my character and a bunch of different things, how I went about my injury. I think that was just a little added [motivation].”</p><p></p><p>Williams’ rant on Thursday provided material for national talking-head morning shows on television — and popular corners of the internet — Friday morning and all through the weekend. Williams undoubtedly was aware of that, though he claimed Tuesday that he “didn’t really see the reaction” from national outlets.</p><p></p><p><b>“</b>I mean, everything I say, somebody’s gonna say something — national or anything like that,” he said. “So didn’t see it. I’m gonna always be myself. I’m gonna speak when I feel I need to speak up — and that was just one of those moments.”</p><p></p><p>The issue, of course, is what Williams <i>didn’t</i> say in that moment. In a four-minute opening statement, Williams said that “every single” report about the severity of his hamstring injury was wrong. When he was asked to clarify the details of his hamstring injury, he refused, saying the media was “not deserving” of the right answer. That was where Williams’ airing of grievances started to feel petty.</p><p></p><p>If he keeps playing well, though, few will care. Williams wasn’t the first Bears quarterback to complain in front of a microphone, of course. The difference is that he has a chance to become known for something more than that..</p><p></p><p>If Williams keeps playing the way he did in Sunday’s win against the Falcons, when he posted a 111.2 passer rating, he’ll build up equity his predecessors never had.</p><p></p><p>In my 14 seasons covering the Bears, I've learned that, when it comes to quarterbacks, fan patience is usually just as long as their leash on the field.</p><p></p><p>Jay Cutler, after all, might have been the original NFL meme: an eye-rolling, smirking caricature that cried out for the Internet — remember Tumblr? — to put a fake cigarette in his mouth and complete the look of ennui.</p><p></p><p>On the field, Cutler was perfectly average. He won 51 regular season games with the Bears — and lost 51. In a Bears career that ran from 2009-16, he won one playoff game — and lost another. In the loss, Cutler’s toughness was questioned just the way Williams’ was. He was diagnosed with a sprained knee — the Sun-Times called it a Grade 2 — and was criticized even by Mike Ditka afterwards.</p><p></p><p>Mitch Trubisky had his own issue with talking heads. In 2019, he said that he wanted the televisions turned off inside Halas Hall “because you've got too many people talking on TV about us and what they think about us -- what we should do, what we are and what we're not.” The Bears went 5-3 the rest of the year and decided not to exercise Trusbisky’s fifth-year option. They went 8-8 the following season before Trubisky left via free agency to become a Bills backup.</p><p></p><p>In Sept. 2023, Justin Fields said he wanted to play “less robotic” and stop over-thinking. Asked why he was over-thinking things, he said it “could be coaching,” adding that “when you’re fed a lot of information at a point in time and you’re trying to think about that info when you’re playing, it doesn’t let you play like yourself." After Fields’ comments blew up over the next few hours, Fields pulled reporters to his locker after practice and claimed he was “never going to blame anything on the coaches.”</p><p></p><p>Fields finished the season 5-8 — and his Bears career 10-28 — before being traded the following offseason so the Bears could make room for Williams. Bears fans are thrilled with that development. Williams struggled mightily in the rainy loss to the blitz-happy Vikings. But in the two full games he’s played this season, Williams has looked as good as he has at any point in his Bears career.</p><p></p><p>Williams' perceived slights helped him return Sunday — and play well. So did the awareness of his own limitations. When he stayed in a clean pocket rather than take off to run, Williams went 24-for-24 for 248 yards, per NFL Next Gen Stats, the most any NFL quarterback had completed without a misfire in at least eight years.</p><p></p><p>Williams, who was challenged by coach Ben Johnson to complete 70% of his passes, leads all passers with at least 50 throws with a completion percentage of 72.5%.</p><p></p><p>That, he said, can carry over Thursday against the Patriots.</p><p></p><p>So will the extra motivation Williams took from his time off.</p>

entries.title: Victims in Mundelein murder-suicide shooting identified
entries.summary: <p>Mundelein police have released the identities of five people killed in an apparent murder-suicide this week.</p><p>Five adults, all related, were found dead after a concerned family member called for a well-being check in the 200 block of Wellington Street around 11:45 p.m. Sunday, Mundelein police said.</p><p>The Lake County Coroner's Office identified the deceased as 80-Year-old James Schmidt, 77-year-old Rebecca Schmidt, 22-year-old Maclaine Schmidt, 37-year-old Nicole Heiser and 51-year-old Bryan Schmidt. </p><p>Bryan Schmidt is believed to be the alleged perpetrator, police said.</p><p>He allegedly shot his four family members before turning the gun on himself, Mundelein police said the preliminary investigation found.</p><p>Multiple suicide notes were left by Bryan Schmidt and found on the scene, police said. The shootings are believed to have taken place between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Sunday.</p><p>Police said they have not had any prior contact with Bryan Schmidt and are working to determine the motive for the shooting.</p><p>Anyone with additional information on the incident is asked to call the Mundelein Police Department at 847-968-4600.</p>

entries.title: Key takeaways from the only Senate debate between Juliana Stratton and Don Tracy
entries.summary: <p>U.S. Senate candidates Juliana Stratton and Don Tracy used an hourlong debate on Tuesday night to show just how far apart their policies are on everything from the minimum wage to immigration and tariffs.</p><p>Stratton, the Democratic candidate for the Senate seat left vacant by Sen. Dick Durbin’s retirement, also repeatedly vowed to stand up to President Donald Trump’s policies, as Tracy, the Republican, used the platform to call her a socialist — three times.</p><p>Here are some key takeaways from the only Senate debate between Stratton and Tracy.</p><h3>What should the minimum wage be?</h3><p>Stratton made headlines during the March primary for proposing a $25 federal minimum wage, far higher than her Democratic opponents thought was possible. On Tuesday, she stressed that a $7.25 federal minimum wage isn’t enough for anyone to take care of themselves or their family. She called $25 an hour a “livable wage, not just the bare minimum, where people can have a little more money in their pockets.” Stratton also said she supports a millionaire’s tax.</p><p>Asked by WTTW moderator Brandis Friedman how that hike would be paid for, Stratton said small businesses would be at the table for any discussions about raising the minimum wage, just as Illinois did when Gov. JB Pritzker and Stratton raised Illinois’ minimum wage from $8.25 to $15 an hour.</p><p>“We worked with the business community, and we raised it incrementally over four years,” Stratton said.</p><p>Tracy, former chair of the Illinois Republican Party, called a $25 minimum wage “a death sentence for small businesses everywhere.”</p><p>“What will that do to the cost of living? What will that do to the cost of a cheeseburger, a Big Mac,” Tracy said. “...Every solution they have is spending more money and raising the cost of living.”</p><h3>Their positions on tariffs</h3><p>The two candidates were asked how the Senate should respond to Trump’s tariffs, with Tracy saying, “the jury’s still out on tariffs.”</p><p>“I like the fact that the president recognizes that we’ve been subsidizing the world, and we’ve been taken advantage of by the world with unfair trade practices out there, and so he’s trying to use, I think, tariffs as a tool, not an objective, but as a tool to reset world trade policy and make it a more level playing field.”</p><p>Stratton shot back at Tracy’s response, reminding him that the U.S. Supreme Court in February ruled that sweeping tariffs Trump imposed in a series of executive orders were illegal. </p><p>“That is not the jury still being out. And with these illegal tariffs, refunds are owed. But guess who’s getting them? Is it you, the people of Illinois? No," Stratton said. "These refunds are going to big corporations like Amazon. That’s who’s getting the refund.”</p><p>Stratton said, if elected, she’d fight to make sure refunds go to the people and not corporations.</p><p>“It has caused chaos. It has caused a trade war with our allies, and that is not the kind of leadership we need,” Stratton said.</p><h3>Immigration and Operation Midway Blitz</h3><p>Stratton supports abolishing ICE and accused Tracy of supporting Operation Midway Blitz. She said she also wants to see a “real path to legal citizenship, including for Dreamers.”</p><p>Tracy called Operation Midway Blitz “ugly and chaotic,” but he compared the immigration enforcement in the Chicago area to that in Memphis, where he said things had “gone pretty well” because local authorities cooperated with federal immigration agents.</p><p>He blamed the violence on “massive resistance by the local authorities,” and he accused Americans of caring more about the deaths of four Americans at the hands of federal agents than to police shot in the line of duty.</p><p>“Certainly the immigration advocates don’t care about the thin blue line,” Tracy said.</p><p>Stratton said Trump didn’t go after the “worst of the worst.”</p><p>“Donald Trump went after tamale vendors and daycare workers, our neighbors,” Stratton said. “And so I'm always going to stand up and speak out when we are seeing people getting killed in the streets by a federal agency.”</p><h3>The Trump factor</h3><p>Tracy repeatedly said that Stratton would “do everything she can to impeach” Trump in her first two years in office. Stratton has said she’d support impeaching Trump, but she has also pointed out the difficulty in doing so because it would take a two-thirds majority in the Senate. Tracy is echoing a GOP talking point going into the general election — as Republican candidates try to paint a picture of Democrats hell-bent on impeaching Trump instead of focusing on other issues.</p><p>“I’m starting to wonder if my opponent is running against me or against the president,” Tracy said in response to a question about conservation efforts.</p><p>Stratton shot back at Tracy, saying that he’d “welcome” an endorsement from Trump.</p><p>“So when I talk about Donald Trump, that’s someone whose endorsement you’re looking for,” Stratton said.</p><p>Tracy said he “never said that.”</p><p>“If the president of the United States would want to endorse me as a candidate, I would accept that,” Tracy said.</p><h3>The scourge of Alzheimer’s</h3><p>The candidates both disclosed that they had lost family members to Alzheimer’s. Stratton has frequently mentioned that she was a caretaker for her mother, Velma, whom she lost in 2016. Stratton on Tuesday said her mother’s health battle inspired her to run for the Illinois House in 2016, to help fight for healthcare for seniors amid massive cuts during the state’s budget impasse.</p><p>Tracy said he admired Stratton for caring for her mother, and said his father also died of Alzheimer’s. He said he also lost his godfather and a brother to the disease as well.</p><p>“This is a horrible disease and we need to do something about it,” Tracy said.</p>

entries.title: University of Chicago to hold public safety meeting after recent sexual assault allegations
entries.summary: <p>The University of Chicago will hold a public safety meeting Tuesday evening in light of recent sexual assault allegations at fraternity houses. </p><p>The meeting will take place from 6 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. at 6054 S. Drexel Ave. and attendees can also <a class="Link" href="https://airtable.com/appWrWmubWT1O3pPm/pagyAo6jPcVKEdFSQ/form" target="_blank" >join virtually</a> via Zoom. </p><p>Meanwhile, a second woman has come forward this week saying she was was sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago fraternity party. </p><p>When the 19-year-old woman went to a University of Chicago fraternity party in February, a member of the frat allegedly greeted her at the door and encouraged her to take a shot of alcohol.</p><p>It left her feeling “unsteady and lightheaded,” and she was ultimately left “alone and unconscious” inside a bedroom at the Alpha Delta Phi house, according to a lawsuit she filed this week against the fraternity's local and national organizations.</p><p>The fraternity brother had assaulted “her limp body” after welcoming her into the sprawling, Collegiate Gothic-style house, 5747 S. University Ave., according to the lawsuit.</p><p>As the attack happened, other fraternity members blocked the woman’s friends from getting to the bedroom, the lawsuit says.</p><p>The accuser, who attends a different university, is identified only as “Jane Doe” — the same anonymous title attached to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/08/lincoln-park-high-students-walk-out-jane-doe-cornell-rape-case" >a woman who recently filed a lawsuit</a> accusing Cornell University frat members of a gang rape.</p><p>That case set off a firestorm that has now engulfed the University of Chicago, where another woman reported she was sexually assaulted at an off-campus party hosted by a different fraternity earlier this month. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >That report of sexual assault</a>, which made national news, is linked to a party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house, 5625 S. University Ave., just a block from the Alpha Delta Phi house.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-0a0000" name="html-embed-module-0a0000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>A university spokesperson said the new allegations in the lawsuit are “disturbing” to its community.</p><p>“The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The University is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the fraternity. The University will cooperate by providing information and is prepared to help the Chicago Police Department in its investigation.”</p><p>The accuser reported the Feb. 7 assault to Chicago police the following day, according to the lawsuit. But months later, the police investigation remains pending and she's received no information from the university, according to her attorney.</p><p>“She's doing the best that she can to help herself,” the woman’s attorney, Michael Grieco, said in an interview. “I think she's been galvanized in a way by others coming forward, and I think that's made her want to do this even more so and create change.”</p><p>The lawsuit identifies her “assailant” as Kevin Shim, although he isn’t named a defendant. No criminal charges have been filed in connection with the alleged assault.</p><p>Shim didn’t respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Alpha Delta Phi’s national organization said Shim was suspended from the fraternity after the organization became aware of the allegations, which it takes "extremely seriously."</p><p>“The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” spokesperson Steve Ehrfurth said in a statement. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a assault and how Jane Doe quickly reported it to police.</p><p>A friend helped her leave the Alpha Delta Phi house, but she struggled to speak and walk as she was led out, according to the lawsuit. The next morning, Jane Doe discovered bloodstains in her underwear and went to police to make her report.</p><p>That investigation remains open, according to a Chicago police spokesperson, who said Jane Doe was treated at Illinois Masonic Hospital a day after the assault reportedly happened.</p><p>The University of Chicago Police Department also reached out to the woman and opened their own investigation, the lawsuit says.</p><p>Grieco said the lawsuit aims to target the failures of institutions, not just individuals.</p><p>“There are always perpetrators committing crimes against others. But I think ... what we've seen around the country really is: ‘Why hasn't this been stopped?” Grieco said.</p><p>“Institutions have known for decades that fraternities can go off the rails. … Each instance that occurs is another level of notice to put this school, put these fraternities on guard to say, ‘Hey, we've got to do something about that.’ And that's what this is about.”</p><p>Jane Doe has received no information from the university about actions taken against the alleged perpetrator or the fraternity, Grieco said.</p><p>Her report to Chicago police should have immediately triggered an investigation from the university, according to Grieco. But when the woman asked the university for the internal records, she was told to file a subpoena, he said.</p><p>The lawsuit names the university as a respondent in an effort to obtain those files.</p><p>It highlights an alleged history of sexual assault at the Alpha Delta Phi chapter that dates back almost two decades.</p><p>In 2009, there were multiple reports of sexual assault at the Alpha Delta Phi house, according to the lawsuit, which says the Chicago and University of Chicago police departments opened investigations in response to a report of sexual assault during the fraternity’s weekly “Bar Night” party.</p><p>Then, in 2022, an Instagram user posted an anonymous account of a sexual assault that allegedly happened at the Alpha Delta Phi house.</p><p>The lawsuit insists the fraternity’s national headquarters is “aware of past instances of sexual assault and investigations of sexual assault inflicted by its members.”</p><p>“If you are a student there at the fraternity, then these fraternity policies and procedures should be in place,” Grieco said. “And the University of Chicago needs to do a better job of ensuring that these places are safe for their students that they know are going there and living there on a day-to-day basis."</p><p>Abba Diallo, a 25-year-old sociology major from West Africa, said she "would like to see the university caring a bit more about the students, especially the young girls."</p><p>"They want to be safe," Diallo said while walking through the campus Tuesday. "They want to know that the university cares about them and their health and their safety, and that we are making sure that we have conversations about content and relationships and all those things. entries.title: I'm not shocked that systems fails sexual assault survivors
entries.summary: <p>Since the story broke about<a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/nyregion/cornell-jane-doe-letter-president.html?eafs_enabled=false" target="_blank" > Jane Doe at Cornell University</a>, I’ve heard a lot about how shocking it is: the gang rape she alleged, the inaction by men in that group chat, the disappointing response by the prestigious institution and the decision by prosecutors not to bring charges. While I couldn’t possibly know all the facts of what happened in that fraternity house, in the police station or throughout the Title IX investigation, I know she was failed by many people who could have helped her.</p><p>More recently, two alleged sexual assaults at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >University of Chicago fraternity houses</a> have captured headlines, and again, caused shock and outrage. As an attorney who's spent 10 years representing student survivors of sexual harm, I am unfortunately not shocked by any of it.</p><p>Every day I witness — and try to mitigate — the harm student survivors experience. While it no longer surprises me, I’m struck by how often survivors tell me engaging with our systems has been equally or more traumatic than the sexual violence itself. And it’s the result of multiple systems failing them, including our culture, schools, government and legal processes.</p><p>So many people, well-meaning and otherwise, ask why more survivors don’t come forward or why they don’t do so immediately. It’s because they know what they’ll face if they do.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4d0000" name="module-4d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Not only are student survivors rightfully afraid of not being believed or being blamed for their own assault, they must also contend with risks of countercomplaints or defamation lawsuits brought by their perpetrators. Recently, I’ve noticed a marked increase in respondents filing complaints against my clients, alleging that they are the real victims. In those instances, survivors must prove not only that they were assaulted, but also that they didn’t assault the individual who harmed them. I understand the strategy: Survivors might drop their case, or the school will say it’s murky, and no one will be found responsible.</p><p>If survivors move forward with their case, the institution investigates and typically holds a hearing. Both parties make statements and answer questions from decision makers and the parties’ chosen advisers, who can be almost anyone. Questions simply must be relevant; courtroom rules of evidence don't apply, and both parties share accounts of what happened without much limitation. It’s a structure that not only sets the stage for theatrical and retraumatizing interactions, but also offers a window into dangerous misunderstandings of sexual harm and its victims.</p><p>What I hear in these cases is chilling. There’s concern over ruining a young man’s life, always with little regard for the life already damaged by the assault he perpetrated. Or arguments that, because her clothes weren’t torn and nothing was broken in her room, she cannot have been assaulted. Declarations that security footage depicting a survivor collapsing in tears after her alleged assault was melodramatic and therefore staged. Explanations that she said “no” but didn’t seem to mean it, or she didn’t say anything at all when she should have. Assertions that if she had truly been assaulted, she would've screamed or clawed his eyes out or broken up with him or made a report sooner. </p><p>That she led him on, or willingly kissed him, or chose to be alone with him, or was out late and chose to drink alcohol — and what did she expect? The strategy is to paint survivors as unstable, or vengeful, or promiscuous, or compulsive liars, or attention-starved.</p><p>Winning a Title IX case as a complainant is an uphill battle. And if the respondent is found responsible, there’s no guarantee regarding outcomes. While respondents in some of my cases were expelled, that isn't the norm. They might be suspended. They might be placed on probation. They might be required to engage with educational content — or write an essay. They might be prohibited from holding campus leadership roles. And the survivors must decide whether they can continue at that institution, knowing they’ll likely be forced to encounter their assailant even after their school determined they committed sexual misconduct against them.</p><p>Survivors deserve better. Proposed state legislation, House Bill 4990, would amend the Preventing Sexual Violence in Higher Education Act to allow Illinois survivors to sue institutions that have failed them, fundamentally improving survivor rights and remedies. This is necessary for real accountability.</p><p>Students deserve to live without fear of being harmed. And if they are harmed, they shouldn’t have to fight to prove they’re good and worthy victims. They deserve processes that center the truth about what harm and trauma look like, not victim-blaming myths and misinformation.</p><p><i>Christina Zuba is a managing attorney at the Chicago Alliance Against Sexual Exploitation, where she has been representing student survivors of sexual harm since 2016.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-730000" name="module-730000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: With gas prices skyrocketing, can electric vehicles actually save you money?
entries.summary: <p>Soaring <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/why-gas-prices-high-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>gas prices</u></a> have been a constant concern since the war on Iran started in February. But many electric vehicle owners are insulated from the pain at the pump.</p><p>Yet, is it worth it to buy an electric vehicle, especially after federal tax credits ended last year? There are many online resources to research whether to purchase an EV. But what are some general pros and cons of owning one? (Learn about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2026/10/20/gas-chicago-5-gallon-does-buying-a-hybrid-make-sense" target="_blank" >hybrid vehicles here</a>.)</p><h3>Is charging an EV cheaper than filling your gas tank?</h3><p>According to <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/hybrids-evs/will-an-electric-car-save-you-money-a9436870083/" target="_blank" ><u>Consumer Reports</u></a>, “the cost of charging an EV is almost always hundreds of dollars less per year than the fuel costs for a similar gas-powered vehicle.” But charging costs depend on the price of electricity and gasoline where you live and the type of EV and battery.</p><p>Consumer Reports has a <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/compare/" target="_blank" ><u>car comparison tool</u></a> that shows how gas and electricity costs will add up over five years based on vehicle type.</p><p>In Chicago, gasoline prices are generally high. For example, the <a class="Link" href="https://gasprices.aaa.com/?state=IL" target="_blank" ><u>average price</u></a> for regular gas hit $5.05 on Tuesday and $6.86 for diesel. The national average was $4.29.</p><p>Meanwhile, residential electricity prices in Chicago averaged $14.91 per kilowatt-hour in October, while the average national rate was $17.41, according to data website <a class="Link" href="https://poweroutage.us/electricity-rates/il/chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Power Outage</u></a>. Electricity rates vary according to the electric company, plan and time of day.</p><p>The cost of charging an EV is determined by multiplying the electricity rate by battery capacity, said <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoev.com/how-much-does-it-cost-to-charge-an-ev/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago EV</u></a>, a company that installs chargers.</p><p>For example, a Tesla Model 3 has a 50 kWh battery. If the local electricity rate is $0.15 per kWh, then a full charge would cost $7.50, according to Chicago EV. The Tesla Model 3’s range is about 240 miles on a full charge. So it costs just over 3 cents per mile to drive.</p><p>Compare that to about 32 miles per gallon for a standard Toyota Corolla, which translates to 15 cents per mile if gas is $5 per gallon.</p><h3>Federal tax credits are gone, but are there other financial incentives?</h3><p>The One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12625?__cf_chl_tk=me39dlOaCEcY65G_3K8ojlWURF8qFwY.hqDd_SbQ4kyw-1790882359-1.0.1.1-7HChWDax9ZlA33_f3KUDjSl9tPk3Rdy51txgi8txqY4" target="_blank" ><u>ended federal EV tax credits</u></a> of up to $7,500 in September 2025. Last year, EV sales spiked ahead of the deadline, then fell to 6.5% of U.S. car sales in the third quarter, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/q3-2026-ev-sales-report-commentary/" target="_blank" ><u>Cox Automotive</u></a>. </p><p>Meanwhile, sales of hybrid EVs sharply increased this year. Nearly 25% of all vehicle sales in the third quarter were electrified, including hybrid EVs and plug-in models, said Cox. <b> </b></p><p>But Illinois still offers EV rebates ranging from $2,000 to $4,000 depending on income, as well as $1,500 for electric motorcycles. The latest cycle for the rebate program began Aug. 1 and will be open until Dec. 31 or until funds run out, according to the Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://epa.illinois.gov/topics/ceja/electric-vehicle-rebates.html" target="_blank" ><u>Environmental Protection Agency</u></a>. The program <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoissenatedemocrats.com/caucus-news/49-senator-dave-koehler-news/4236-koehler-backed-electric-vehicle-rebate-program-opens-in-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>started in 2022</u></a> under the state’s Climate and Equitable Jobs Act.</p><p>Eligible Illinois residents who buy an EV that costs less than $80,000 from a licensed Illinois dealer may qualify for a rebate.</p><p>In addition, <a class="Link" href="https://www.comed.com/about-us/clean-energy/electric-vehicle-charger-and-installation-rebate" target="_blank" ><u>ComEd</u></a>, the Chicago-area electric utility, offers rebates on Level 2 home charging stations for eligible residents. Maximum rebates range from $750 to $2,000 depending on income. ComEd’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240201470793/en/ComEd-Encourages-Residential-Customers-to-Apply-for-New-EV-Charger-and-Installation-Rebate" target="_blank" ><u>rebate program</u></a> started in 2024.</p><p>EV charger installation costs vary, but buying and installing a Level 2 home charger in Illinois can cost roughly <a class="Link" href="https://www.reliant-electrical.com/ev-charger-installation-cost-illinois/" target="_blank" ><u>$1200 to $2,500</u></a>, according to local contractor Reliant Electrical. Older homes might need wiring upgrades that could add <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/hybrids-evs/buying-guide/#will-a-hybrid-phev-or-ev-save-me-money" target="_blank" ><u>thousands more</u></a>.</p><h3>Is it more expensive to buy an EV than a gas-powered car?</h3><p>Yes. The average price for a new EV was $56,126 in July, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/ev-market-monitor-july-2026/" target="_blank" ><u>Cox Automotive</u></a>. That was, on average, $6,477 more than a new conventional gas-powered vehicle. For used EVs, the average price was $37,832 as of July.</p><p>Tesla led U.S. sales of EVs, followed by Rivian, Hyundai, Toyota and Cadillac.</p><p>Automakers may also offer <a class="Link" href="https://www.edmunds.com/electric-car/tax-credits-rebates-incentives/" target="_blank" ><u>rebates and discounts</u></a>, so check with them.</p><h3>What kind of range do EVs have?</h3><p>Today, electric vehicles typically have ranges of 200 to 300 miles on a full charge, according to auto insurer <a class="Link" href="https://www.insureonthespot.com/worth-buying-electric-car-chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>Insure on the Spot</u></a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.caranddriver.com/features/g32634624/ev-longest-driving-range/" target="_blank" ><u>Car and Driver</u></a> tested 10 EVs driving at 75 miles per hour. Their range varied from 280 miles for a Rivian to 410 miles for a Lucid Air and 400 miles for a Chevrolet Silverado.</p><p>Longer road trips require planning to map charging stations along the route. Fast charging stations can replenish an EV’s battery to about 80% in roughly 30 minutes, said Insure on the Spot. But keep in mind that cold temperatures, like those Chicago winters, can temporarily reduce an EV’s range by 20% or more.</p><h3>Is it hard to charge an EV? Where can you charge them around Chicago?</h3><p>For those without home chargers, finding charging stations requires planning. Several websites and apps have maps of EV charging stations in the Chicago area, such as <a class="Link" href="https://chargehub.com/en/map?_gl=1*1yt47wa*_up*MQ..*_ga*NjE5MDYwMDUyLjE3OTE0OTA3OTU.*_ga_NSMWTMS73N*czE3OTE0OTA3OTQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTE0OTA3OTQkajYwJGwwJGgzNjUyNjg0NzY." target="_blank" ><u>ChargeHub</u></a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://data.cityofchicago.org/Environment-Sustainable-Development/Map-of-Public-Electric-Vehicle-Charging-Stations-i/euxu-dxsh" target="_blank" ><u>city of Chicago</u></a>. Other apps include PlugShare, GRID.com and EVgo.</p><p>As of October 2024, Chicago had 860 public EV charging stations with 4,829 charging ports, according to the city’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/cdot/supp_info/CDOT_EVFramework/CDOT_EVFramework.html#docaccess-bd54dff96248d2ada4bad633c05e51b7" target="_blank" ><u>Department of Transportation</u></a>. Chicago had fewer chargers per vehicle than the country, state and county. In Cook County, there were nearly 49,000 EVs, as of this August, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/content/dam/departments/vehicles/statistics/electric/2026/electric081526.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois data</u></a>.</p><p>Getting an EV charger in a condo or apartment building requires approval from the building manager or landlord. In the five-year period from 2020 to 2024, 75% of new Chicago apartment buildings offered EV charging, said <a class="Link" href="https://chargehub.com/en/countries/united-states/illinois/chicago.html" target="_blank" ><u>ChargeHub</u></a>. They are more common in newer residential buildings in neighborhoods such as River North, West Loop, Fulton Market and Gold Coast.</p><h3>Is it more expensive to insure an EV?</h3><p>Generally, yes. Insuring EVs can cost 10% to 20% more than conventional gasoline cars because they are more expensive to fix or replace after an accident, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.insureonthespot.com/worth-buying-electric-car-chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>Insure on the Spot</u></a>. But many EVs have advanced safety features that might qualify owners for insurance discounts.</p><p><b>Are EVs cheaper to maintain?</b></p><p>Generally, yes. EVs have fewer moving parts and don’t need oil changes. EV maintenance and repair costs are about <a class="Link" href="https://atlaspolicy.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Comparing-the-Cost-of-Owning-the-Most-Popular-Vehicles-in-the-United-States-2025-Update.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>40 percent lower</u></a> than comparable gas vehicles, said the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nrdc.org/stories/electric-vs-gas-cars-it-cheaper-drive-ev" target="_blank" ><u>Natural Resources Defense Council</u></a>.</p><p><b>What are the environmental and health impacts of EVs?</b></p><p>EVs help cut air pollution. In Cook County, on-road transportation accounts for 58% of total greenhouse gas emissions, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/progs/env/drive-electric-chicago.html" target="_blank" ><u>City of Chicago</u></a>. But EVs don’t emit tailpipe emissions, making them cleaner compared to gasoline or diesel vehicles, especially if charged with renewable energy such as solar.<br></p>
entries.author: Amy Yee

entries.title: Restrict surveillance systems before America falls down an Orwellian abyss
entries.summary: <p>The palm-lined streets of Pasco County, Florida, might seem worlds away from the blustery Chicago winters, but they share a chilling commonality: Both have used predictive policing against their most vulnerable residents.</p><p>For years, the Pasco County sheriff’s office ran a predictive-policing program using algorithms to assemble lists of residents supposedly destined to commit future crimes. Deputies identified “prolific offenders” — a misnomer since these individuals had not committed crimes — who faced relentless, warrantless harassment designed to drive them out of the county. Only after <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/press-release/case-closed-pasco-sheriff-admits-predictive-policing-program-violated-constitution/" target="_blank" ><u>protracted litigation</u></a> by the Institute for Justice did the sheriff concede constitutional violations, shutter the program and agree to a six-figure settlement in late 2024.</p><p>While one might expect progressive Chicago to reject such tactics, the city's police department had a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2020/1/27/21084030/chicago-police-strategic-subject-list-party-to-violence-inspector-general-joe-ferguson" >database that used analytics</a> to predict which residents were most likely to be involved in shootings — as either the shooter or the victim. The Chicago Police Department's approach perhaps wasn’t as aggressive as Pasco County’s but similarly yielded no meaningful drop in crime. The program was decommissioned in 2019.</p><p>But the problem of surveillance persists. </p><p>Across the country, law enforcement agencies have begun outsourcing the Fourth Amendment’s requirement of individualized suspicion to opaque software and automated tracking networks. As my Cato Institute colleague Matthew Cavedon recently <a class="Link" href="https://www.hks.harvard.edu/faculty-research/policy-topics/science-technology-data/democracy-happening-fight-over-flock-cameras" target="_blank" ><u>pointed out</u></a>, automated license plate readers “aren't license plate readers anymore; they’re people readers at this point.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1b0000" name="module-1b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Proponents insist that law-abiding Americans have nothing to fear because police have no interest in our daily routine, touting plate readers as vital investigative and deterrent tools. Yet where dragnet databases exist, abuse inevitably follows. The Chicago area is no exception.</p><p>In Naperville, Officer Oscar Maldonado is accused of using the Flock database to <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/patrick-dowhen-says-naperville-police-officer-oscar-maldonado-used-flock-cameras-stalk-starting-affair-fiance/19859406/" target="_blank" ><u>track the movements</u></a> of his girlfriend's ex-fiance. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" >William Copp</a>, a former Holiday Hills police chief and part-time Prairie Grove officer, used Flock to stalk his former partners and others, according to McHenry County prosecutors. And just this month, Illinois State Police said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/07/former-joliet-police-officer-charged-over-alleged-flock-camera-misuse" >Jeremy Harrison</a>, a former Joliet lieutenant, also abused Flock.</p><p>Maldonado, Copp and Harrison aren't alone in their alleged actions. Across the country, the Institute for Justice has documented over <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/the-ij-database-of-alpr-abuse/" target="_blank" ><u>270 </u></a>license plate reader abuses nationwide. </p><p>Flock <a class="Link" href="https://itemlive.com/2026/09/07/editorial-more-cops-are-accused-of-misusing-flock-cameras-this-is-becoming-too-much-like-big-brother/" target="_blank" ><u>defends its cameras</u></a> by claiming they merely “capture what anyone could already see standing on the street,” focusing on "the vehicle, not the person." The fiction that a fully integrated, 24/7 camera grid merely replicates a patrol officer on a street corner ignores scale and permanence. No human officer could track millions of drivers simultaneously, preserve their historical travel patterns indefinitely and recall their movements with a single keystroke.</p><p>This dragnet functions in tandem with the proliferation of the criminal code and a Supreme Court that has blessed pretextual traffic stops. Under prevailing Supreme Court precedent doctrine, an officer needs only a minor traffic or equipment violation — an air freshener dangling from a rearview mirror or a busted taillight — to stop someone based on race or ethnicity.</p><p>Federal agencies routinely exploit this dynamic. U.S. Border Patrol has been <a class="Link" href="https://www.military.com/dhs-program-analyzes-americans-finances-to-flag-drivers-for-traffic-stops-report" target="_blank" ><u>operating a secret program</u></a> analyzing our financial records and travel patterns to flag everyday drivers as suspicious, passing the tips to local police. Local police can then trail the target until they go 1 mile over the speed limit, pull them over and question and search citizens who never suspect that the routine traffic stop was actually orchestrated by Border Patrol.</p><p>But the cooperation goes much further than just traffic stops, as WBEZ's Lisa Kurian Philip recently pointed in her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/09/to-protect-immigrant-students-a-chicago-area-college-told-flock-to-remove-its-cameras-the-company-refused" target="_blank" >report </a>detailing how federal immigration authorities have accessed Flock data at Elgin Community College and other Illinois colleges.</p><p>Enacting strict guardrails on automated surveillance tech is a necessary first step, but administrative patches will not shield Americans from Big Brother. At an absolute minimum, lawmakers must require law enforcement to obtain a judicial warrant before querying license plate reader databases.</p><p>Yet even a warrant requirement does not cure the fundamental danger of an omnipresent camera network recording our every movement. The framers enacted the Fourth Amendment out of aversion to general purpose warrants — the reviled writs of assistance that granted British authorities broad, suspicionless power to inspect anyone at will. Pervasive, automated surveillance resurrects that very practice in the modern era.</p><p>As we commemorate our nation’s<sup> </sup>250th birthday, we should remind ourselves that we were born out of a desire for freedom from a tyrannical government. The founding premise of the American constitutional order is that the government must justify its intrusions to the citizen, not that the citizen must justify his daily movements to an algorithm. If lawmakers don’t reassert that boundary today, the freedom to navigate public life without suspicion will exist only in memory.</p><p><i>Mike Fox is a legal fellow with the Cato Institute’s Project on Criminal Justice.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3c0000" name="module-3c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Animals in the wild are worthy of personal pronouns
entries.summary: <p>I was so pleased to read Sun-Times reporter Robert Herguth’s recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/outdoors/2026/10/12/birds-of-prey-adapting-chicago-illinois-raptors-utility-poles-cellular-towers-eagles-hawks-osprey" >story </a>about the growing presence of raptors in the Chicago area, which you can easily see for yourself while driving down the road. We have an enormous responsibility to watch out for our wild brethren and do better than our country did before when the law allowed people to poison these magnificent birds with chemicals and destroy habitat and food sources at an unimpeded rate. Too much harm is still happening, but federal law curtails many toxins, and there is a widespread effort by hundreds of agencies and organizations across the country to restore much-needed natural lands, including here. Alerting the public to these beings’ presence builds important support for their protection.</p><p>Another way to assist osprey, owls, eagles and everybody else in nature is to join the growing ranks of scientists and advocates who recommend providing animals with their proper pronouns. In 2021, In <a class="Link" href="https://www.idausa.org/about/support-ida/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=1447838534&gbraid=0AAAAADgw0QRDS0WZNpLX-rRfxu6xJpGfa&gclid=CjwKCAjw_9bWBhBGEiwAomyTIrKa-Ew5A3MzNUp4882cFtiQ8VO0Y70uarUxmRPvEBGivohMChE02RoCqM4QAvD_BwE" target="_blank" >Defense of Animals</a> and<a class="Link" href="https://animalsandmedia.org/" target="_blank" > Animals & Media</a> partnered to urge the Associated Press to update its style guide to use personal pronouns. They were joined by over 80 animal advocate leaders from across the globe, including Jane Goodall and the Center for Biological Diversity. According to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.idausa.org/campaign/guardian/latest-news/jane-goodall-joins-in-defense-of-animals-call-for-ap-stylebook-update/" target="_blank" >news release</a>, “The scientific consensus is that nonhuman animals are conscious beings — some<i>one</i> not some<i>thing</i> — and the language we use should reflect that.”</p><p>At Friends of the Chicago River, where we work to protect people, water and wildlife every day, we already took that to heart, and our people and publications refer to "he, she, them or who” over "it." This formal adaptation to our style guide is out of respect for the wild lives with whom we share our watershed and our desire to see them treated as having value with inherent rights of their own.</p><p>In a time when the climate crisis, habitat loss and a new force of political threats pose such danger, it will help if we use the right language, which tells everyone wild animals of any kind are not inanimate objects.</p><p><i>Margaret Frisbie, executive director, Friends of the Chicago River</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9f0000" name="module-9f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Airbrushing Blagojevich’s past </h3><p>I find it astonishing that ousted Illinois Gov. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/rod-blagojevich" target="_blank" >Rod Blagojevich</a> continues to receive national television exposure, particularly on Fox News, as though his disgraceful record in public office were merely an unfortunate misunderstanding.</p><p>I remember a very different Blagojevich.</p><p>My late mother, Judy Baar Topinka, challenged him for governor in 2006. I witnessed the personal attacks, ridicule and vilification directed at a woman who devoted her life to serving Illinois. Political disagreement is legitimate. Attacking someone's character for political advantage is something else entirely.</p><p>Blagojevich was impeached, removed from office by a unanimous 59–0 Illinois Senate vote, and convicted of federal corruption offenses. Presidential clemency cannot rewrite history or erase the betrayal of public trust.</p><p>My mother believed public office was a responsibility, not a personal possession. She worked across party lines, respected political opponents and understood that serving people mattered more than personal publicity.</p><p>Television networks have every right to interview Blagojevich. But giving him a national platform without confronting his record does a disservice to viewers and to the people of Illinois.</p><p>This is not about Republicans or Democrats. It is about character, integrity and accountability.</p><p>My mother spent her life earning the public's trust. Blagojevich squandered his.</p><p>Illinois should never forget the difference.</p><p><i>Joseph Baar Topinka, New Braunfels, Texas</i></p><h3>Vote to keep Trump in check </h3><p>To me, only a simple analysis is needed to decide whom to vote for in the upcoming congressional elections.</p><p>If you are happy with how things have gone since Jan. 20, 2025, voting for Republicans makes sense.</p><p>However, if you think that Donald Trump has behaved like a monarch and been a domestic and foreign policy vandal, is not that competent or qualified for the job in a conventional sense and is more than a little corrupt, you might want to vote for people who will work to constrain his worst tendencies.</p><p>This leads to another question: What evidence have Republican senators and representatives presented that they would do that, especially in the context of Trump's project to purge the party of those who disagree with him having progressed substantially during his reign?</p><p>Some Republican members of Congress support what Trump is doing because they agree with it. Some acquiesce because they want to keep their jobs. If Republican voters want to rehabilitate their party — and they should not kid themselves about whether this is needed, both for the party, itself, and for the nation — they must show on Election Day that failing to fall in line with their party's leader isn't the only way that those who represent them in Congress could lose their jobs.</p><p><i>Curt Fredrikson, Mokena</i></p><h3>Homophobic name-calling </h3><p>Recently JD Vance made a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/us/politics/vance-talarico-attacks.html?eafs_enabled=false" target="_blank" >false homophobic comment</a> implying that James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, was gay. This is our vice president? Of course, Vance minions giggled like grammar school kids. I wonder if one of Vance's kids were gay how he would feel about all the laughter.</p><p><i>Thomas Bajorek, Burbank</i> </p><h3>Uncertainty of life </h3><p>A priest from Ecuador was giving a sermon on how fleeting life is over the weekend when a crucifix fell off its stand, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/world/ecuador/priest-ecuador-dies-crucifix-falls-livestreamed-mass-rcna604211" target="_blank" >killing him</a>. If that tragedy isn't a quintessential example of irony, I don't know what is.</p><p><i>Wes Dickson, Orland Park</i><br></p>
entries.author: Letters to the Editor

entries.title: Put in the work to equip Americans in manufacturing jobs
entries.summary: <p>America wants to make more things here at home. But there is a basic constraint we do not talk about enough: A factory is only as useful as the people who know how to run it.</p><p>Manufacturing employed <a class="Link" href="https://www.bls.gov/charts/employment-situation/employment-and-average-weekly-earnings-by-industry-bubble.htm" target="_blank" ><u>more than 12.6 million Americans in August</u></a>, including <a class="Link" href="https://www.bls.gov/eag/eag.il.htm" target="_blank" ><u>more than 571,000 in Illinois</u></a>. The Bureau of Labor Statistics expects <a class="Link" href="https://www.bls.gov/ooh/Production/" target="_blank" ><u>nearly 870,000 openings in production occupations each year</u></a> over the coming decade, largely as workers retire or leave those jobs. And if U.S. factories returned to their highest utilization rates of the last decade and employment rose proportionally, <a class="Link" href="https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/operations/our-insights/ready-to-ramp-how-us-manufacturers-can-scale-at-pace" target="_blank" ><u>McKinsey estimates</u></a> manufacturers would need about 1.4 million additional workers.</p><p>That is not an argument against bringing manufacturing back. It is an argument for getting serious about the workforce needed to make it happen.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9e0000" name="module-9e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Before I joined Congress, I studied mechanical engineering and ran small businesses developing technology in national security and renewable energy. That experience taught me something our economic policy too often forgets: We treat a new machine, software or factory as an investment, while too often treating the worker who can operate and improve that technology simply as a cost.</p><p>We need to change that in three ways.</p><p>First, we need to train people for the jobs that actually exist.</p><p>Georgetown University researchers estimate an <a class="Link" href="https://cew.georgetown.edu/cew-reports/bridging-middle-skills-gap/" target="_blank" ><u>annual shortage of nearly 712,000 certificates and associate degrees</u></a> aligned with high-paying middle-skill occupations through at least 2032, including more than 360,000 in blue-collar fields. Workers in the occupations they studied earn a median of $83,300 by midcareer.</p><p>But producing more credentials is not enough. In half of American labor markets, Georgetown found that <a class="Link" href="https://cew.georgetown.edu/cew-reports/greatmisalignment/" target="_blank" ><u>at least half of middle-skill credentials would need to be in different fields</u></a> to match projected demand. We have a training shortage, but we also have a matching problem.</p><p>That is why, during my first term in Congress, Rep. Glenn Thompson, R-Pa., and I introduced the bipartisan <a class="Link" href="https://edworkforce.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=401634" target="_blank" ><u>Strengthening Career and Technical Education for the 21st Century Act</u></a>, which became law in 2018 and strengthened connections between career education and in-demand jobs.</p><p>We can see that approach in Illinois. Elgin Community College opened a new Manufacturing and Technology Center for students training in advanced manufacturing, automation, robotics, welding and other technical fields. I helped secure <a class="Link" href="https://elgin.edu/about/campus-visitor-information/mtc/ecc-receives-2-million-in-federal-funding-for-manufacturing-and-technology-center-.php" target="_blank" ><u>$936,000 for the school’s mechatronics and automation programs and another $2 million for advanced manufacturing equipment</u></a>, helping students train on industry-standard technology for jobs employers actually need to fill.</p><p>Second, when businesses invest in technology, they need to invest in workers too.</p><p>Automation, robotics and artificial intelligence can make American factories more productive, but they also change the skills workers need. U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., and I introduced the Investing in American Workers Act to provide a <a class="Link" href="https://www.warner.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/warner-krishnamoorthi-introduce-legislation-to-help-workers-adapt-to-ai-driven-economy/" target="_blank" ><u>20% tax credit for increases in qualifying worker-training expenses</u></a>, including apprenticeships, community college programs and career and technical education.</p><p>If we recognize the value of upgrading the machine, we should recognize the value of upgrading the worker’s skills alongside it.</p><p>Third, we need to judge people by what they can actually do.</p><p>Millions of Americans gain valuable skills through community colleges, apprenticeships, military service or years on the job. Too many still hit the paper ceiling because employers require a four-year degree even when it is not necessary to do the work.</p><p>That matters especially in manufacturing, where technical ability, training and experience can matter more than whether a worker has a bachelor’s degree.</p><p>Companies increasingly announce moves toward skills-based hiring, but changing a job posting is easier than changing who actually gets hired. Research from Harvard Business School and the Burning Glass Institute found that the additional opportunities created by such policies amounted to fewer than 1 in 700 hires at the companies they studied.</p><p>I was also proud to co-author the bipartisan Skills-Based Federal Contracting Act, which is establishing a new standard requiring federal agencies to justify degree requirements for covered contractor positions instead of using them by default.</p><p>A four-year degree remains the right path for millions of Americans and many careers. But it is not the only path to a good job, and it should not substitute for determining whether someone has the skills to do the work.</p><p>We need people trained for the jobs we are creating, businesses that keep investing in their skills and hiring systems that recognize what workers can actually do.</p><p>We know how to invest in machines. If America wants a manufacturing comeback, we need to get just as serious about investing in the people who make them productive.</p><p><i>U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Illinois, serves Illinois’ 8th Congressional District, which includes the northwest suburbs.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7a0000" name="module-7a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Husband's interest wanes after wife's surgeries
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been married to my husband for many years. We are both over 60. About eight years ago, I was diagnosed with, had surgery for and rehabbed from a benign brain tumor. It left me with considerable facial paralysis that I had further surgery to repair — all in all, 10 facial surgeries.</p><p>Since my initial tumor surgery, my husband has had little to no interest in intimacy. It has been seven years since we have been intimate. His health does not prevent it. I have tried gently discussing the issue with him, telling him I feel it is due to me. He says it's not but gives no clear reasons.</p><p>We are living like roommates. Our relationship otherwise seems as compatible as before. I am not sure how to approach this issue anymore. Any insight or wisdom? — <i>PERPLEXED IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR PERPLEXED:</b> That must have been a frightening and difficult time — it's good to know you've made it past the worst of it. Because your intimacy issues began with a medical event, I recommend finding a certified sex therapist who specializes in illness and injury.</p><p>The American Association of Sexuality Educators, Counselors and Therapists (aasect.org) can connect you with a variety of professionals, many of whom offer a telepractice option. Try to get your husband to attend a few sessions with you. Even if he won't, you can go alone to learn how to regain your confidence and manage any lingering effects of the surgeries.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've struggled with mental illness all my life. I am schizoaffective, but I take my medication and now know what it's like to live a relatively "normal" life. My problem? That would be my friend "Sharon." She also suffers from mental illness, but it's not well controlled even though she says she takes her meds.</p><p>Every three months or so, Sharon finds something wrong with what I've done or said and sends me a rudely worded "breakup" email or message. A few days later, she realizes what she's done and apologizes, saying she won't do it again, but she does do it again.</p><p>The last time was the straw that broke the camel's back for me. After reading what she wrote, I took the high road and didn't respond. I decided that being her friend is too hard since she's repeated the same behavior several times. I blocked her from my email and Messenger, and got on with my life.</p><p>Abby, she's not taking "no" for an answer. She created a new email address to contact me, basically begging me to come back and be her friend. I feel torn. While I understand it's her illness causing the behavior, it's terribly hurtful. Do you think I should take her back or let sleeping dogs lie? — <i>TORN IN WASHINGTON</i></p><p><b>DEAR TORN:</b> Either let sleeping dogs lie or understand that the price of a friendship with Sharon will be accepting the fact that she periodically goes off the rails. If you can learn to take it less personally, being her friend may not be as draining.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

The show starts with extreme highs but recedes in success from there, and rather surprisingly can’t find an ending which, in my experience, often comes off as the most moving and memorable in Shakespeare’s canon.</p><p>The first half of this show, though, is unquestionably some of the most exciting Shakespeare I’ve seen in some time. After establishing a happy tone in its early moments, it shifts suddenly into a propulsive psychological thriller, as King Leontes (Demetrios Troy) has what we would call a mental break with the flick of a light cue.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “The Winter’s Tale” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e00000" name="module-e00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through Dec. 12th<br><b>Where</b>: Chicago Shakespeare Theater, 800 E. Grand Ave.<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoshakes.com/productions/2627-winters-tale/" target="_blank" ><u>Tickets</u></a> from $65-$125; run time is 2 hour and 50 minutes with one intermission.</div> </div><p>Initially encouraging his lifelong best friend and fellow king Polixenes (Chiké Johnson) to extend his visit, he instantly becomes convinced that his guest is having an affair with his queen, the eminently virtuous and currently pregnant Hermione (Jessica Dean Turner). His paranoia — so wrong and yet so unstoppable — becomes a landslide of tyrannical terror, as one previously trusted aide after another attempts, and fails, to dissuade him from a determination to punish the innocent.</p><p>These scenes can come off as repetitive and even frustrating given how unjustified Leontes’ beliefs are, but here they couldn’t be more fully engrossing and frightening.</p><p>As Leontes, Troy genuinely listens to his advisors before rejecting them, which gives his character dimension. We see in his darting eyes the moment his mind hits a brick wall that blocks his executive functioning. In response, his advisors (all excellently played by Erik Hellman, Ronald L. Conner, Sean Fortunato and Kevin Gudahl) each must up the desperation of their pleas, giving every rejection a growing sense of dread.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Hermione’s desperation and Issy van Randwyck, as Hermione’s strongest defender Paulina, delivering a certainty that almost competes with Troy’s Leontes, along with a decidedly spunky attitude.</p><p>By the end of this first half, Leontes has realized his error — an early deus ex machina does the trick — but the damage is irreversible. In this late, “mature” Shakespeare, some mistakes can’t be fixed but can only be partially healed, and only with time. Thus, we jump forward 16 years during intermission.</p><p>After the break, we move into full-on comic mode, and Hall turns it up to eleven, a “Spinal Tap” reference that’s apt here given that Autolycus (Fortunato), one of Shakespeare’s famous rogues, enters as an Ozzy Osbourne-type clad in leather and fur. We also get the ensemble dressed as sheep and playing in the rock band “Sheep Trick” (silly and amusing!) and an innocent shepherd (Gudahl) and his son (Dan Haller) donning Southern accents to represent their naivete (less amusing and overly stereotypical).</p><p>And we don’t just get a shift in tone, but in directorial approach, as if the two sides of representing life in this change also represented two sides to Hall as a director of Shakespeare.</p><p>The first half was stripped down yet fully realized, a single, clear concept executed with style and intensity. The comic section feels overburdened with ideas, albeit some extremely clever. Autolycus is a former courtier turned outcast, and here he’s a walking satire on glamor (not unlike Osbourne himself). It borders on brilliance as an idea, but as executed it’s just too much, producing a chaotically farcical rather than gently pastoral comedy. Fortunato in this case puts forth such a relentless, even desperate, need to please the audience that the antics end up clouding the many scenes he drives.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Sean Fortunato (center) portrays an Ozzy Osbourne-type Autolycus.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Kyle Flubacker</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What’s lost is the underlying tale that we need to care about to get us to some form of integration. In this case, it’s the unlikely courting of Perdita (Felicia Oduh), who has been raised by the shepherds and doesn’t know she is actually Leontes and Hermione’s daughter, by Florizel (Estaban Ortiz-Villacorta), Polixenes’ princely son. But the couple feel like afterthoughts amidst the chaos.</p><p>The effect of this cascades into what should be an emotional, fantasy-ish ending. Here, the production feels neither intensely focused nor idea-oriented, but simply perfunctory and bland. Even what seems like obvious opportunities established by Michael Pavelka’s quite lovely set, or Hall’s initial framing sequence of this show as a children’s story, seemingly get abandoned.</p><p>All that said, in addition to the outstanding first half of “The Winter’s Tale,” the good news here is that this same cast — really an excellent ensemble — will be back, running this play in repertory with “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” which opens next month.</p>

entries.title: Singer and chef Lizz Wright merges her talents at The Hunt in Woodlawn
entries.summary: <p>Lizz Wright never imagined releasing an album and opening a café in the same week. </p><p>“I learned to mind what you ask for,” she jokes. “I’m exhausted but so grateful.”</p><p>On Sept. 22, the jazz chanteuse and professionally trained chef and her wife, Monica Haslip, opened their newest spot, The Hunt, 915 E. 60th St., at the Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts on the campus of the University of Chicago. It builds off their other business, Carver 47 Food & Wellness Market at Little Black Pearl Art & Design Center, 1050 E. 47th St., established in 2017.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0c0000" name="image-0c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf25151/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6271x3519+0+331/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2F1f%2F7b1538b846f9959ab0d975afe8be%2Flizzwright-261021-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9bd711a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6271x3519+0+331/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2F1f%2F7b1538b846f9959ab0d975afe8be%2Flizzwright-261021-15.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/72a26e6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6271x3519+0+331/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2F1f%2F7b1538b846f9959ab0d975afe8be%2Flizzwright-261021-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chef Lizz Wright (left) and Monica Haslip, who created and designed The Hunt at Logan, smile in the restaurant at the Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts in Hyde Park, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. It builds off their other business, Carver 47 Food & Wellness Market at Little Black Pearl Art & Design Center, 1050 E. 47th St., established in 2017.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Opening the doors to The Hunt came just three days before Wright released her latest album, “Nearness,” a collection of standards and spirituals recorded with her longtime music collaborator, pianist Kenny Banks Sr.</p><p>While managing both worlds sounds like a challenge, for the multihyphenate talent, she finds a lot of crossover. “I really want to practice composing every day of my life,” she said, seeing parallels between writing a song and creating a dish.</p><p>In fact, she and Haslip (who spent years at BET and Johnson Publishing before embarking on youth-and-art center Little Black Pearl) first met when Wright performed a concert at the Hyde Park staple during a concert in 2013 and they instantly connected on ideas for collaboration. Wright even named her Virginia-based label, Blues & Greens Records, to show the synergy between her two pursuits, which collided around the same time early in life.</p><p>As the daughter of a pastor in small-town Georgia, Wright started her music journey as a child by singing in the choir and eventually became the music director of her dad's church. By 2002, she went pro and signed a deal with Verve Records; the following year, her debut album “Salt” topped Billboard's contemporary jazz charts.</p><p>Like music, Wright's love of cooking was fostered at a young age, when she tended to the family garden. A desire to pursue food took her to New York, where she graduated from the Natural Gourmet Institute in 2009. From there, she headed to the mountains of western North Carolina where she spent her time honing her food craft on 27 acres of farmland. “A lot of my food and plant relationship inspiration comes from there,” she said. “I really love the way [Southerners] make biscuits. I love the way they can put a whole breakfast on top of salad greens. I love the time being taken to really eat a real breakfast, and that it’s available all day.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure homemade quiche, buttermilk and cheddar scallion biscuits and a build-your-own breakfast sandwich. The Hunt also highlights flavors from different cuisines in sandwiches like the Bloom “V-ahn Mi,” a vegan bánh mì with fried tofu and pickled vegetables on a baguette, and the BBQ jerk salmon burger on a brioche bun.</p><p>“We are really trying to cater to people who are using their minds a lot,” Wright said of the menu, which includes a range of breakfast, lunch and snacks and grab-and-go items to get people through long days of creative work.</p><p>For those needing a mental break, the university spot, which is open to the public, also features record players that spin some of Wright and Haslip’s vinyl collection. </p><p>“I'm really enjoying the dialogue that this space is creating,” Wright said of the way food, music, art and community intersect at The Hunt. </p><p>The interaction with customers harkens back to her church roots. “I really like seeing people every day or every week and knowing their names,” she said. “It’s like I’m nourishing people in my own way.”</p><p>Wright also does so with a range of fresh juices and smoothies like the Green Glory Juice (a mix of apple, spinach, celery, ginger, lemon and parsley) that have been a signature of Carver 47 and were just In another example of interconnectedness, Wright’s music has been featured on former President Barack Obama’s annual playlists, including “Hit the Ground” on this summer’s edition.</p><p>Wright and Haslip are conscious of the history and people who hail from the Hyde Park/Kenwood area (where they also live) and have named both of their cafés after similar luminaries. Carver 47 is named for agricultural scientist, educator and inventor George Washington Carver. </p><p>“We realized he was at Tuskegee [Institute] for 47 years and thought that was wild since [the café is] at 47th and Greenwood,” said Wright. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf4288c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5825x3269+0+307/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Fa7%2F13c7e8e44ab28b90e3eb39a4b2e4%2Flizzwright-261021-24.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/db6691e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5825x3269+0+307/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Fa7%2F13c7e8e44ab28b90e3eb39a4b2e4%2Flizzwright-261021-24.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf4288c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5825x3269+0+307/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Fa7%2F13c7e8e44ab28b90e3eb39a4b2e4%2Flizzwright-261021-24.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>On the menu at The Hunt is a sandwich called The Sculpture in homage to artist Richard Hunt, with blackened chicken thigh, smoked Gouda, pickled red onion, charred red pepper relish and garlic aioli on a brioche bun. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“He just passed [in 2023], so I still feel like his presence is so fresh in this neighborhood,” Wright said. On the menu at The Hunt is a sandwich called The Sculpture in homage to him, with blackened chicken thigh, smoked Gouda, pickled red onion, charred red pepper relish and garlic aioli on a brioche bun. Haslip also designed custom wallpaper for the space that pays tribute, “but it’s very subtle and you have to get up close,” said Wright, adding, “We also have a collection of different pieces of art and artifacts that he collected from places around the world.”</p><p>In a way, Wright sees these figures as her third set of creative collaborators, behind Haslip and Banks Sr. “What I really love about it is that these rooms that are designed to tell someone's history, to show what they loved, to show what they gave and how they contributed to the world,” she said. “I feel like it introduces the humanity of these great American icons with such tenderness and really without agenda. We’re just here.”</p>
