entries.title: Fearing ICE, some Chicago immigrants shift work, daily life to nighttime hours
entries.summary: <p>Before leaving home, even to do his laundry at a nearby laundromat, Gustavo Dominguez says a prayer. He asks God to let him return home safely.</p><p>It was evening as Dominguez, 49, and his wife Patricia Dávila, 67, loaded their laundry bags into the trunk of their car and headed out. Dominguez does not have legal status. His wife has work authorization and says she sought asylum after fleeing threats in Mexico.</p><p>They now wait until nighttime to do their laundry and to buy their groceries. They’re afraid of encountering Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents during the day.</p><p>At the laundromat, Dominguez hurriedly unloads the bags of laundry. Dávila helps, talking as she works. Dávila has noticed a lot more people now come to do their laundry at night.</p><p>“You’ll see — [ even] more people start arriving later,” she says in Spanish.</p><p>Once the wash is in, the couple leaves to buy groceries at a nearby supermarket as darkness settles over the neighborhood.</p><p>Inside, piñatas hang overhead. Giant tamale pots line a high shelf alongside coolers. Each pushes a cart, covering different parts of the store to finish the shopping faster.</p><p>Dávila says she often sees young people on video calls with their mothers, holding up products and asking which brand to buy.</p><p>There is "so much fear that they send the kids to do the shopping,” she says.</p><p>Nearly a year after Operation Midway Blitz officially ended, immigrants in Chicago are still changing their work schedules and fitting everyday errands into the hours after dark or before dawn out of fear they’ll be arrested or detained by ICE. Workers described buying vending supplies before sunrise, working at night, shopping at night and cutting back on trips outside their homes. Some still work during the day because their livelihoods depend on it, but change their hours when they can. The shift has meant lost income, and the constant anxiety continues to take a toll on mental health and relationships.</p><h3><b>‘People of the night’</b></h3><p>From the beginning of 2026 through the first week of August, ICE made 1,560 arrests in Cook County, according to a Chicago Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis of ICE arrest data obtained by the Deportation Data Project. Legal and community groups have documented encounters at courthouses, schools and grocery stores, saying operations have become less publicized but continue to happen as part of the Trump administration's ongoing mass deportation campaign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d70000" name="html-embed-module-d70000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30622243"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30622243/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>“We’re becoming <i>gente de la noche" — </i>[people of the night], says Baltazar Enriquez, president of the Little Village Community Council. “We do things at night now.”</p><p>Enriquez says he knows many immigrants who have taken the night shift as a way to try to avoid encounters with ICE. One mother told him she struggles to sleep after working nights. She still has to get her children ready in the morning after she gets home. He recalled her describing stretches of only two or three hours of rest, catching naps when she could.</p><p>“I’m getting dark circles under my eyes,” he says she told him.</p><p>Rosemary Magaña, a therapist and program director at the Coalition for Immigrant Mental Health, says nighttime routines can cost people social connections that help them cope. Visits, weekend outings and gatherings fall away.</p><p>Magaña has felt the vigilance herself. During the early days of Midway Blitz, she would return from driving her son to school, from watching cars and imagining what she would do if agents stopped them. Once, she says, her neck became so stiff she could not move it.</p><h3><b>Agents prompted new nighttime routine</b></h3><p>Dávila says their new nighttime routines began after they saw immigration agents detain people near their home. During one incident<b> </b>last fall, agents passed close to their windows as a girl on a skateboard warned residents not to come outside. Agents knocked her off the board, according to Dominguez, who says she heard loud bangs and that tear gas canisters landed behind their home and in front of a neighbor’s house.</p><p>Dominguez covered the windows with blankets. They locked the doors and turned off the lights. He feared agents would come inside. Through September and part of October 2025, they tried to stay inside.<b> </b>For about a month, a friend with legal status drove Patricia to do laundry and buy groceries. Gustavo continued going to work, but stopped driving himself.</p><p>During those early months of Midway Blitz, he paid for Uber rides to work, sometimes lying down in the back. Dominguez works in a warehouse and loads trucks. When his shift ended, he waited hours for a co-worker to take him home. A second Uber cost too much.</p><p>He grew anxious and lost weight, maybe 10 to 20 pounds Patricia says. She worries about him.</p><p>Dávila fled death threats in Mexico after reporting sexual abuse of girls and helping people flee violence. In 2010, two of her nephews were killed in a student massacre. Now, she fears staying in Chicago and returning to Mexico.</p><p>“I’m caught in [between] the crossfire,” she says.</p><p>Still, she credits her involvement in community organizations with helping her find some sense of protection when things get overwhelming.</p><p>But she sees her husband struggling more with the fear, still anxious and angry about what they witnessed last fall.</p><p>Gustavo has a U.S. sports team shirt he can no longer bring himself to wear.</p><p>“The admiration I felt for this country has turned into contempt,” he says in Spanish.</p><p>He speaks about seeing parents being mistreated by agents in front of their children, about the pain children might carry long after an arrest.</p><p>“You’re their hero, and they treat you like that?” he says. “But what they want is to strip you of your dignity.”</p><p>Aside from the anxiety, there are also financial pressures. The couple has put aside enough money for about two months of rent in case one of them is detained.</p><p>They used to go to the mall for clothes and other things they needed, Patricia says. Now, she orders more online, buying clothes through the online site Shein and household and personal items through Amazon. Shopping this way can cost more, she says. She misses finding deals in person.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4c0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Patricia Dávila says their new nighttime routines began after they saw immigration agents detain people near their home one day last fall.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Losing sleep</b></h3><p>At Cook County Health, psychiatrist Dr. Hugo Solari hears daily from patients living in fear of ICE.</p><p>“Every day in practice, I hear patients discussing how they had to adapt their lives in order to avoid encountering ICE,” Solari says.</p><p>Some request telehealth appointments or prescriptions by mail. Others postpone preventive care because they fear leaving home.</p><p>The stress also interrupts their sleep. Anxiety makes sleep difficult, and lost sleep deepens the anxiety. For patients moving activities into nighttime, getting enough regular sleep can become harder still. Over time, Solari says, the chronic stress and disrupted sleep can affect physical as well as mental health.</p><h3>Moving work into the night</h3><p>Imelda, a childcare worker who doesn’t have legal status, now only takes evening babysitting jobs. Imelda is a pseudonym. The Sun-Times is not using her real name because she fears deportation.</p><p>She takes great pride in her work, helping teach children how to treat others. She especially enjoys caring for children up to age 3.</p><p>“I like to plant empathy in them, respect for all people,” she says in Spanish.</p><p>When immigration operations began last fall, Imelda was caring for a young girl as a nanny. She still took her to museums, parks and the library, watching for agents as she went. Nannies and babysitters called one another to share warnings about agents near the parks and libraries where they took children, urging co-workers to avoid those areas and take care.</p><p>But at work, Imelda tried to keep her fear from showing.</p><p>“Even with my whole body trembling, I had to be professional at work,” she says.</p><p>Imelda told the girl’s mother how frightened she felt. Her employer changed her work arrangement. The family also offered to shelter Imelda and her family in their home. The offer made her feel that they valued her work and cared about her.</p><p>It reminded her of Anne Frank.</p><p>That job ended when the girl started school. Now, Imelda takes occasional evening babysitting jobs helping children through meals, showers, books and bedtime. The work keeps her indoors, but she works only about twice a month.</p><p>Imelda had thought of herself as someone others could turn to. Through her volunteer work in workers’ rights, she represents people and speaks up for them. Among fellow workers, she is the one who sings, dances and tries to help everyone relax. But lately, she is surprised by her own fear, by how difficult it has become to leave home.</p><p>But even staying home doesn’t quiet the fear.</p><p>Footsteps upstairs make her think agents have entered the building. She imagines someone letting them in. She considers where she could hide. Outside, she studies passing vehicles for signs they might belong to immigration agents.</p><p>Magaña, the therapist, says prolonged anxiety can change what people expect from the world. They anticipate danger and doubt that circumstances will improve. She describes it as systemic trauma, reaching beyond those directly detained.</p><p>“It doesn’t have to happen to you for it to traumatize you,” she says.</p><p>Imelda tries to stay strong for her children and reassure them that nothing will happen. But they are afraid, too, she says. Trips to the park and time playing outside have become less frequent. She worries about children taking on concerns about food and rent when they should be able to focus on their studies.</p><p>“All of this is going to leave lasting effects,” she says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1f0000" name="image-1f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ae6403a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2F08%2Fd7fb39cd46f1adce2ded9ff428a3%2Ficenight-2610250251.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b16696c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2F08%2Fd7fb39cd46f1adce2ded9ff428a3%2Ficenight-2610250251.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8eac54f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2F08%2Fd7fb39cd46f1adce2ded9ff428a3%2Ficenight-2610250251.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Guillermo Flores tends to customers. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8eac54f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2F08%2Fd7fb39cd46f1adce2ded9ff428a3%2Ficenight-2610250251.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/912b8c9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2F08%2Fd7fb39cd46f1adce2ded9ff428a3%2Ficenight-2610250251.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8eac54f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2F08%2Fd7fb39cd46f1adce2ded9ff428a3%2Ficenight-2610250251.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Guillermo Flores tends to customers. He sometimes stays home and doesn’t work if he fears an encounter with ICE.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Shopping before sunrise</h3><p>Guillermo Flores, 54, was among the first to arrive at the street vendors association’s monthly meeting. He took a seat as other vendors trickled in.</p><p>Flores has sold food from a small pushcart for about 16 years. He prepares cups of mango, watermelon, pineapple and cucumber before heading out with raspados, chips and chicharrones.</p><p>He has a vending license and pays taxes, he says. He has held a driver’s license for more than 14 years without an accident or having it revoked.</p><p>“I’m trying to do everything correctly,” he says in Spanish.</p><p>Still, reports of immigration enforcement in his neighborhood often keep him from selling. He stays home for a day, then sometimes another, losing income.</p><p>Avoiding daytime work altogether would mean giving up the business he has spent years building. Instead, he changes the parts of his day he can. He used to buy supplies around 7 a.m. Now, he shops at 5, before sunrise, hoping to avoid an encounter. He continues selling during the day but for fewer hours.</p><p>Some vendors prefer to work near one another so they can help and exchange warnings, he says. Where he sells, there is only one other vendor nearby.</p><p>For Flores, moving his selling hours into the night would bring a different risk. He fears robbery and avoids staying out after dark.</p><p>“We have to protect ourselves from ICE, and we also have to protect ourselves from robberies,” he says.</p><p>When he sees it getting dark, he leaves.</p><p>“I say thanks to God and whatever sold, sold, and let’s go,” he says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Rosemary Magaña, a therapist and program director at the Coalition for Immigrant Mental Health, says nighttime routines can cost people social connections that help them cope. Visits, weekend outings and gatherings fall away.<br></p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Finding support</h3><p>Magaña hears especially from women who care for everyone else while keeping their own distress from showing. They worry that appearing frightened will frighten their children, too.</p><p>“You can cry and struggle and also help others,” she says.</p><p>Support begins with being believed, Magaña adds.</p><p>“Find spaces that do believe you, validate you and normalize your stress,” she says. “That don’t call you paranoid.”</p><p>A weekly therapy appointment isn’t always enough. She spoke about cooking together, sharing food and finding people who listen without dismissing the danger. The coalition offers <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/" target="_blank" ><u>free virtual support circles</u></a> for immigrants and those supporting them.</p><p>“I’m here to support you in whatever is going to work best for you," she says.</p><p>Back at the grocery store, Patricia and Gustavo find a shorter checkout line and quickly join it. Their clothes are still at the laundromat. They have to return and dry them before they can go home.</p><p>For those errands, they go together. But work takes them in separate directions.</p><p>At work, Patricia cleans hotel rooms while waiting for Gustavo’s text confirming he has reached his warehouse job at 10 a.m. If his message does not come around the usual time, he told her, she should understand that he has been taken.</p><p>He rarely used to text. Now, Patricia has saved a year of his daily messages:</p><p>“I’ve arrived.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Keenan Chen</i></p>

entries.title: Illinois’ electric grid is under a lot of stress. What does that mean for consumers?
entries.summary: <p>On the afternoon of Aug. 12, 1999, a blackout roiled Loop businesses, knocking out power at the Chicago Board of Trade before markets closed, darkening office buildings and trapping people in elevators. Traffic lights were out as cops tried to direct traffic. It was chaos.</p><p>No one expected this blackout, which lasted 11 hours in some spots.</p><p>Mayor Richard M. Daley was furious at the electric company, ComEd.</p><p>“This company has to go down to ground zero and start all over again, get rid of all your engineers, bring contractors in, bring outside engineers. This is an emergency,” Daley fumed.</p><p>ComEd admitted the mayor was right, and the utility went to work to improve the decades-old grid.</p><p>No more blackouts.</p><div class="Enhancement" centers rapidly multiplying to power artificial intelligence.</p><p>According to some estimates, the number of data centers has doubled in the last few years. Around 5,000 data centers are operating, under construction or proposed across the country, according to industry estimates. That includes more than 100 in northern Illinois, and almost everyone needs enough electricity to power a midsize city.</p><p>Data centers require every bit of electricity that Illinois power sources — nuclear, coal, natural gas, wind and solar — can produce.</p><p>ComEd customers are seeing higher bills, in large part because data centers are expanding everywhere. Even as ComEd continues to spend money on improving the electric grid, the high demand for power is setting up a potential crisis.</p><p>Let’s take a step back to understand how all this works.</p><h3><b>The grid explained</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The electric grid is really just the poles, transmission lines and other equipment that helps move electricity to our homes and businesses from power plants.</p><p>For instance, nuclear power is created at one of six plants in Illinois. It’s sent through power lines, stopping at different substations along the way that control the amount of power that gets delivered to your house.</p><p>More than half the energy used in Illinois comes from nuclear sources.</p><p>When power is created by a plant or by a wind or solar farm, it’s delivered through equipment owned by ComEd in northern Illinois.</p><div class="Enhancement" </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Chicago belongs to a multistate power consortium</b></h3><p>The generation and delivery of electricity are two separate operations and have been for decades.</p><p>Chicago and the northern Illinois grid is connected to a dozen other states across the eastern United States, as well as Washington, D.C. The arrangement, in place since 2004, allows states to give or take power from partners in what’s known as the PJM Interconnection grid. PJM buys power for supply across the multistate consortium.</p><p>Top of mind for PJM is making sure there is plenty of power even when demand is sky-high — like on the hottest day of summer when everyone is cranking air conditioners.</p><p>However, because these data centers require enormous amounts of energy, the price of electricity is determined by the needs of this larger pool of states. ComEd customers began seeing their bills go up in 2025.</p><h3><b>Nuclear gets a lifeline</b></h3><p>Just six years ago, nuclear plants in Illinois were in danger of closing because power demand wasn’t growing.</p><p>That’s all in the past.</p><p>Inside the Byron Nuclear Power Plant near Rockford recently was even noisier than normal, with huge pieces of equipment being moved in for a large-scale maintenance operation.</p><p>The plant is scaling up with $355 million in improvements so it can produce even more power.</p><p>Newer, more efficient equipment “will provide a higher output,” plant manager Shane Harvey says.</p><p>These improvements are necessary to keep up with the demand for power.</p><p>In Illinois, nuclear plants were hailed early on as highly reliable, producing massive amounts of energy. In recent years, environmentalists have embraced nuclear power as a cleaner source than coal and natural gas, which contribute to climate change.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div The plant is undergoing an upgrade to run more efficiently and produce more electricity.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Pay their fair share</b></h3><p>Today, AI data centers drive up demand for power and the electricity prices that we’re paying.</p><p>It’s a situation so out of hand that President Donald Trump has asked Big Tech executives to <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5985699/trump-self-police-ai-development" target="_blank" ><u>pledge</u></a> to foot the bill.</p><p>Closer to home, Gov. JB Pritzker has stopped giving data center developers financial incentives to build massive power-hungry hubs until Illinois lawmakers pass laws to address soaring electric bills.</p><p>In addition to high power bills for consumers, the data centers threaten one of the governor’s signature accomplishments on climate change.</p><p>In 2021, Pritzker signed into law a measure that eliminates harmful carbon dioxide from power plants by the middle of the century. Carbon, released by coal and natural gas plants, is a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming.</p><p>These fossil fuels will continue to burn, heating up the planet and contributing to respiratory problems in people, until the production of cleaner forms of energy are up and running.</p><p>Related to Trump’s ask of Big Tech, <a class="Link" href="https://grist.org/energy/why-google-is-paying-to-upgrade-nuclear-power-plants/" target="_blank" >Google</a> is investing in five nuclear power plants in Illinois to make sure that the energy continues to flow. It may not be enough: Politicians are talking about mandatory rules that hold the data center developers and owners more accountable.</p><p>Until then, consumers are left footing the bill.</p><div entries.title: Polish poet turns words of Holocaust victims, perpetrators into shards of 'memory activism'
entries.summary: <p><i>    during the war we laid out bodies like wood</i><br><i>    but after the war we laid out wood in the forest  </i><br><i>    like bodies freshly felled.</i></p><p>Grzegorz Kwiatkowski is not Jewish, but reads his poetry like an Orthodox Jew praying, bending at the waist, rocking forward and back.</p><p><i>    I went with my child to the forest and cried helplessly with him</i><br><i>    tears dripped from my eyes and the child wiped them away with his hand</i><br><i>    and I so regretted I had brought him into the world</i></p><p>He's in a third floor conference room at the University of Chicago, reading to about two dozen people, gathered on Monday morning to hear him.</p><p><i>     they didn't know where to run since it was an open field and they ran in circles</i><br><i>     how we laughed</i><br><i>     and before we killed them</i><br><i>     we even whistled some tunes</i></p><p>Kwiatkowski is reading — loudly, with little inflection — from his book <a class="Link" href="https://raintaxi.com/crops/" target="_blank" >“Crops,”</a> translated from Polish by Peter Constantine. More a pamphlet than a book: 19 small, hard, stone-like poems over 32 pages.</p><p><i>     my father</i><br><i>     a decent office worker in the railways</i><br><i>     never took part in any of the shootings</i><br><i>     he was just doing his job</i><br><i>     organizing transports</i><br><i>     eastward and westward</i><br><i>     north and south</i><br><i>     back and forth</i></p><p>The poems are his, but the words aren't — he gathered them from taped testimonies, combining victims, perpetrators and bystanders. </p><p>"I didn't change any of the words," he says. "But still I'm framing it. I'm choosing the fragments. I'm responsible."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-510000" name="module-510000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>I'm here because he sent me "Crops." I read it in less than 10 minutes, but the book rearranged my brain, providing necessary starkness, a counterpoint that I've been missing. Over the years, we've seen the Holocaust transformed into entertainment, especially on social media. Once there was one Anne Frank. Now there are 6 million. The Holocaust has been retrofitted into a bracing tale of courage, resistance, and redemption. The Holocaust is not a tale of courage, resistance and redemption. It is an epic of cruelty, obedience and horror.</p><p>Kwiatkowski agrees.</p><p>"Most art about the Holocaust is kitsch," he says.</p><p>Kwiatkowski gathers words, but doesn't mince them, which makes him a controversial figure in Poland, where depictions of the Holocaust that don't relentlessly depict the Poles as either victims or heroes are highly unwelcome. The Polish government once demanded that the Sun-Times take down a column of mine suggesting otherwise and, when the paper refused, we were sued. We won, because this is America. Whether it stays America...</p><p><i>I was refused because according to them one couldn't write about the occupation this way</i><br><i>they said I was opening the window so narrowly</i><br><i>just a sliver could be seen</i><br><i>that I look at the Holocaust with just one eye</i><br><i>and speak it in a whisper</i></p><p><i>one must write differently about the Holocaust</i><br><i>the window must be thrown wide open and one must shout</i><br><i>not whisper the way I do</i></p><p>Kwiatkowski's poems are shouts; I reproduced only the milder ones, in consideration of sensitive readers. Nobody's head is sawed off here. </p><p>He is from Gdansk, where he founded a rock group, Trupa Trupa. He is currently artist-in-residence at Yale University's Fortunoff Video Archive for Holocaust Testimonies.</p><p>When Kwiatkowski was 9, his grandfather, who had been a prisoner in the Stuthoff concentration camp, returned to the camp for the first time, taking him along, an experience that transformed him.</p><p>"I didn't know what was going on. Later, I felt he gave me one of the most important lessons in my life," said Kwiatkowski. "A very dark one, but I started to ask myself questions: why people are building gas chambers? Why people are building concentration camps? And they're doing it on and on and on. It's a never-ending story, unfortunately."</p><p>We call them "detention facilities" now, and while ICE isn't killing people en masse, the truth is, we don't know what's going on inside those remote facilities, and many Americans don't want to know. If you haven't noticed, we live in a country where ethnic groups are routinely demonized — Somalis in Minnesota, immigrants everywhere — and masked government thugs pull people off the street for no reason at all. The bedrock of any Holocaust.</p><p>Kwiatkowski calls what he does "memory activism," the poems, "the main point of my life."</p><p>Along with his wife and children. Kwiatkowski mentions that his wife, who is Jewish — he didn't know that when they married, he said, calling it her “family secret” — put up a mezuzah on the <i>inside</i> of the front door frame of their apartment. So the neighbors wouldn't see. Because you know how neighbors can be.</p><p><i>most of the townsfolk came to see their murdered neighbors</i><br><i>some lay still alive in the pits</i><br><i>Good morning Mr. Brumberg</i><br><i>Good morning Mrs. Bulkin</i><br><i>Good morning</i><br><i>Good morning</i><br></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydityhtd-l-il/" target="_blank" >LGBTQ+ designers make Chicago Fashion Week history</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydityhtd-l-ir/" target="_blank" >Minju Park</a></h5><p>Each year, Chicago Fashion Week stages creations by local designers through a series of events and runway shows.</p><p>But this year brought a first: More than a hundred attendees gathered at a Wicker Park art gallery last week for the sold-out Queer Couture Runway show. Executive producer Madison Smith and artistic director Emry Yarger said it was the first event in Chicago Fashion Week to explicitly state it was created by queer creatives to highlight queerness in design.</p><p>The show featured nine designers ranging in experience levels and styles. Organizers said the idea for centering the show around queerness came up organically.</p><p>Smith and Yarger acknowledge that queer creatives have always been a part of the city’s fashion scene. They said they wanted to create an environment of openness for up-and-coming designers looking to try new ideas.</p><p>"Black and Brown, queer and trans people set our culture across the board, and that deserves to be honored and recognized" Yarger said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydityhtd-l-iy/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Pizza, Chicago dog and Italian beef aside, what's an essential Chicago dish every tourist or transplant needs to have? entries.title: What the Bears are doing to honor Mike Ditka on Thursday
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will hand out fake mustaches to fans on Thursday night as part of their plan to honor Mike Ditka, who died earlier this month.</p><p>The first 10,000 fans will also receive a Bears knit headband inspired by Ditka's trademark sweater.</p><p>The Pro Football Hall of Fame will put a display in the Soldier Field south courtyard. The Bears will commemorate Ditka will a stencil on the Soldier Field grass. The Bears' spirit squad will hold Ditka-themed flags. </p><p>The team will also hold a moment of silence before the game, which is expected to air live on the "Thursday Night Football" broadcast.</p><p>The Bears will continue to wear Ditka's No. 89 patch over their hearts on their jerseys. </p><p>Thursday marks the Bears' first home game since Ditka died Oct. 9 at age 86. Ditka coached the Bears to their only Super Bowl title during the 1985 season. He beat the same team that the Bears are playing Thursday night: the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/21/bears-patriots-dennis-allen-blitzing-dominated-third-down-thursday-night-football-nfl" target="_blank" >Patriots</a>.</p><p>As a Bears player, Ditka was the first tight end ever inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams wins NFC Offensive Player of the Week
entries.summary: <p>For the second time in his career, Caleb Williams is the NFC Offensive Player of the Week.</p><p>Three days after he beat the Falcons in his return from a three-game absence because of a torn hamstring, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback won the award Wednesday. He went 30-for-36 for 305 yards, one touchdown and a 111.2 passer rating <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/10/21/bears-patriots-podcast-caleb-williams-drake-maye-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >against the Falcons</a>. He went a whopping 24-for-24 from a clean pocket.</p><p>Williams last won the award in Week 3 last year, when he posted a 142.6 passer rating in a home win against the Cowboys.</p><p>Before that, the last Bears quarterback to win the award was Justin Fields after he ran for 178 yards in a game in 2022. </p><p>Williams and Jay Cutler have each won the award twice. No Bears quarterback has ever won the award more than twice. </p><p>Williams said Tuesday he didn't attach any special meaning to the game, his first back since Week 2.</p><p>"I've had some pretty cool games in my career," he said. "It was cool getting back. But I think it was just kind of another game for me.”</p><p>The Bears host the Patriots on Thursday night.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Woman accused of shoving 73-year-old CTA passenger off Loop bus
entries.summary: <p>A Homewood woman is accused of pushing a 73-year-old man to the ground as he tried to exit a CTA bus earlier this month in the Loop. </p><p>Charne R. Sisson, 34, was charged with aggravated battery of a person 60 or older and aggravated battery of a transit employee performing permanent duties or a transit passenger, both of which are felonies, police said. </p><p>Sisson "knowingly and intentionally pushed the victim in the face, causing him to fall to the ground and dislocate his right shoulder," according to court records. </p><p>It happened as the 73-year-old was exiting a CTA bus in the 100 block of North Michigan Avenue on Oct. 5, according to police. </p><p>Sisson, who was arrested on another CTA bus Tuesday after police issued a community alert about her, was scheduled for a detention hearing Wednesday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse. <br></p>
entries.author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi

entries.title: How Dennis Allen's blitzing Bears have dominated third down
entries.summary: <p>If it’s third down Thursday night, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will likely blitz. And it’s probably going to work.</p><p>Nine of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/10/21/bears-patriots-podcast-caleb-williams-drake-maye-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> 17 sacks this season have come on third down. Despite being on the field less than any defense in the sport, the Bears are second in the NFL in third-down sacks.</p><p>As a result, they have the second-best third-down percentage in the NFL. They allow only 25.8% of third downs to be converted, which trails only the blitz-happy Vikings. The Bears allow only 20% of fourth downs to turn into first downs, too, which is also the second-best rate in the league.</p><p>Credit defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, who lives for these moments.</p><p>“He's always been known to have a great pressure package, primarily on third down,” coach Ben Johnson said.</p><p>That’s how a team that allows six yards per play all season — tied for the most in the NFL — is somehow giving up the sixth-fewest points in the league entering Thursday night’s game against the Patriots at Soldier Field. And how a franchise that didn’t add a relevant edge rusher this season — and last week saw its highest-paid player, defensive end Montez Sweat, be suspended for two games — can rank fifth in the NFL in sacks.</p><p>That formula won't work all season long. If the Bears want to compete for a championship, they likely need to find an edge rusher, somewhere, that can contribute on third down. In the meantime, though, what Allen is doing has his flawed defense looking dominant at times. He’s given 68 points in two games this year — and 51 in the other four.</p><p>More than half the Bears’ nine third-down sacks have come by blitzers. Two of slot cornerback Kyler Gordon’s three sacks Sunday came on third downs. Both times, he forced quarterback Michael Penix to fumble.</p><p>The most impressive part was just how quickly it worked. Two of his three sacks Sunday came in under 2.44 seconds, which are the fastest by any NFL player this year. Gordon pressured Penix five times, all within 2 ½ seconds. No NFL cornerback had done that at least 2018.</p><p>The blitzing didn't start when Gordon returned from injury. Allen has blitzed a defensive back 59 times this year, second to only the Ravens. Safety Dillon Thieneman had a third-down sack Sunday. Cornerback Malik Muhammad did earlier this year, too.</p><p>That’s a credit to Allen’s creativity.</p><p>“We’re not just sitting ducks with the offense knowing what we’re going to do,” cornerback Jaylon Johnson said. “When they’re guessing trying to figure out what we’re going to do, it gives us an advantage.”</p><p>Putting the opponent in third down — behind quarterback Drake Maye, the Patriots rank 13<sup>th</sup> in conversion percentage — is the first step. In Year 2 of Allen’s system, the Bears are playing faster because they "understand what we're trying to do at a higher level this year," Johnson said.</p><p>This week will test Allen’s game-planning prowess. With no real practices between games, Allen was forced to come up a plan that his players could learn quickly. Gordon won’t be a secret weapon this week, either.</p><p>Still, Allen still figures to find something exotic. </p><p>“It's really hard to put in a lot of crazy stuff,” Allen said. “So, you try to have some things that maybe the opponent hasn’t seen, and kind of go from there.”</p>

entries.title: Reabre el renovado campus satélite de Malcolm X College con un centro comunitario de $20 millones
entries.summary: <p>Malcolm X College celebró el sábado la reapertura de su ampliado campus del West Side, que incluye un centro comunitario renovado nombrado en honor del representante Danny K. Davis, junto con funcionarios escolares, funcionarios electos de la ciudad y del estado y líderes comunitarios.</p><p>La universidad puso la primera piedra del proyecto de $20 millones para ampliar y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2024/11/11/malcolm-x-college-expansion-austin-health-education" target="_blank" >renovar su campus satélite del lado oeste</a> en el 4624 W. Madison St. en noviembre de 2024. Ahora terminado, el proyecto culminó con una ceremonia de corte de cinta que marcó la reapertura del edificio Malcolm X West Campus.</p><p>El edificio alberga el antiguo West Side Learning Center, que fue rebautizado como el Centro Comunitario Danny K. Davis en agosto. La reapertura del sábado también marcó el regreso de las clases presenciales en el campus, apenas días antes de que los estudiantes de los City Colleges of Chicago tengan programado iniciar la segunda mitad del semestre de otoño.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b30000" name="module-b30000"></a> <div entries.title: One hurt during tire 'issue' while jet lands at O'Hare Airport, airline says
entries.summary: <p>A tire 'issue' erupted as an American Airlines flight from Barcelona landed at O'Hare International Airport Tuesday, injuring one person. </p><p>The accident happened as AA Flight 41 — carrying 234 passengers and 11 crew members — landed, according to a statement from the airlines. First responders assisted and passengers were safely transported to the terminal by a bus.</p><p>One person was taken to a hospital, according to a spokesperson for the Chicago Fire Department. It was unclear if the injured person, who was taken to a hospital in good condition, was a crew member or passenger.</p><p>The aircraft was taken out of service for inspection by the airline’s maintenance team.</p><p>“We thank our team members for their professionalism and we apologize to our customers for their experience,” the airline said.</p>
entries.author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi

entries.title: Northwestern University student apparently drowns in Lake Michigan
entries.summary: <p>The body of a Northwestern University student was pulled from Lake Michigan in Evanston Wednesday morning after a passerby spotted a person in the water. </p><p>The passerby called 911 about 7 a.m. saying the person was in the water near 70 Arts Circle Drive, police said in a statement. That's near the Ryan Center for the Musical Arts and just north of Clark Street Beach.</p><p>Firefighters pulled the unresponsive woman from the water, near the university's southern lakefill area and performed CPR. They rushed her to a local hospital, where she was pronounced dead, police said in the statement. Her name has not been released by the Cook County medical examiner's office, which responded to the scene. </p><p>Evanston and Northwestern University Police worked together to identify the woman as a Northwestern student, who was not from the Evanston area. </p><p>Evanston Police launched a drone to search the southwest and southeast portions of the university’s property and lakefront as part of the investigation, which continues. There is no danger to the Northwestern or Evanston communities and police reminded the public to stay safe as Lake Michigan can be dangerous. </p><p>Hazard warnings and signs prohibiting swimming and fishing are posted along Northwestern University’s lakefront property, according to the statement. </p><p>Evanston Police urge people to follow posted warnings, check lake conditions before approaching the water and follow instructions from city or university officials to stay out of the water and off of break walls and rocks.</p><p>Northwestern University did not immediately respond to requests for comment. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Pope Leo’s doctors say tests show he needs no further treatment for lung cancer
entries.summary: <p>VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo’s doctors say that final tissue and molecular tests have confirmed that his lung cancer was localized and that no further treatment is needed, the Vatican said in a statement Wednesday.</p><p>Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after having the lower lobe of his right lung removed. The surgery confirmed that Leo had <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pope-leo-xiv-lung-cancer-adenocarcinoma-56b1c4fa87864d157eb3999a64f94c87" target="_blank" >lung adenocarcinoma</a>, the most common type of lung cancer.</p><p>The pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the tests on tissue removed during the pope's surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread.</p><p>“A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors said.</p>
entries.author: AP

aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>Last year, Johnson's aldermanic opposition shot down his proposed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/02/mayor-brandon-johnson-plea-for-his-corporate-head-tax-proposal-2026-proposed-budget" >corporate head tax, </a>and instead passed an alternate budget against his wishes. The mayor’s attempt to make the head tax easier to swallow this year by pairing it with a “full rebate” for jobs located in impoverished communities did not seem to soften his opponents. </p><p>“This is like Yogi Berra said: `Déjà vu all over again.’ We don’t know why he’s so insistent on taxing jobs,” said Derek Douglas, president of the Civic Committee of the Commercial Club, one of Chicago's most influential business groups. “We have a growth issue. Any policies that make that worse, we’re gonna oppose and we’re gonna oppose it vigorously. Last year, he did it. It was rejected. He’s back with the same idea again. We hope the City Council will reject it again.”</p><p>Chicagoland Chamber of Commerce President Jack Lavin said the business community will join the Civic Committee in mounting a full-court press to block the head tax and Johnson's proposed cloud tax increase he called "direct taxes on small businesses — not the tax on Big Tech" that Johnson is trying to sell.</p><p>“The cloud tax is essentially a sales tax — and I don’t think there’s anywhere in the nation where there’s a 20% sales tax,” Lavin said.</p><p>“This is on every small business in Chicago and every resident who has software or leases equipment to do work. The tax impacts businesses of all sizes. It’s about technology and leased assets that businesses of all sizes depend on to operate… for digital advertising and all things they need to do to get their product out there.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7d0000" name="html-embed-module-7d0000"></a><div style="min-height:620px" id="datawrapper-vis-ZvwE7"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ZvwE7/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-ZvwE7"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ZvwE7/full.png" alt="A look at Mayor Brandon Johnson’s revenue wishlist (Stacked column chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Mike Ruemmler, president of One Future Illinois, said the non profit-created by business leaders to influence city and state policy is prepared to spend “hundreds of thousands of dollars” to educate voters and their alderpersons. </p><p>“If he would listen to his colleagues on the Council, he would know that a head tax is D.O.A., but... his goal doesn’t seem to be a budget that’s trying to build consensus. It’s a budget about trying to rev up his base to make sure he gets to the runoff," Ruemmler said.</p><p>Zoning Committee Chair Gilbert Villegas (36th) said the proposed 33% ramp-up of the cloud tax that has turned into a cash cow for the city would fall most heavily on “folks using Microsoft 365 who are not millionaires." </p><p>“This is a different version of nickel-and-diming everyday Chicagoans," Villegas said.</p><p>Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th), who chairs the Hispanic Caucus and co-chairs the Progressive Caucus, countered that the cloud tax is “one of the few levers we have." He added that it "should have been raised even higher last year” and he would support the mayor’s proposal to take it to 20%. He also supports the head tax, as he did last year.</p><p>But Vasquez said he is adamantly opposed to Johnson’s plan to borrow $480 million over two years to cover the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/14/city-council-global-settlement-ex-chicago-cop-reynaldo-guevara" >$260.8 million global settlement </a>to 17 plaintiffs framed for murders by corrupt former Chicago police Det. Reynaldo Guevara and other police-related settlements either “expected or approved.”</p><p>“They just tried to bond out to get... $70 million and only got $30 million to close a gap last year. So it’s clear that we’re not able to borrow even when we think can borrow. Our credit ratings keep going down, which makes our ability to borrow even harder. And borrowing to cover more than half the deficit — you’ve got to make the case for how that’s responsible, because I don’t see it," Vasquez said.</p><p>Last year, a 31-member coalition of conservative and moderate alderpersons rejected the corporate head tax and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/23/mayor-brandon-johnson-city-council-alternate-budget" >pushed through an alternative budget</a> that authorized video gambling terminals, selling outstanding debt and other alternative revenues that Johnson opposed and has either been unwilling or unable to implement.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Ferguson said the “single most disappointing… and almost cynical feature” of Johnson’s budget is that there is “literally nothing more than marginal savings and efficiencies.” </p><p>“What are deemed efficiencies is just cover mostly for chopping away at the police department," Ferguson said. "It’s only taking an ax to that, and calling it savings and efficiencies.” </p><p>Johnson has used his first three budgets to shrink the Chicago Police Department by attrition. His fourth budget includes more of the same.</p><p>In a briefing with reporters Tuesday, Acting Budget Director Jonathon Ernst acknowledged that Johnson “froze 500 police officer vacancies” in his 2026 budget and that the city would be “continuing that at a lesser level” next year to cut personnel costs by $34.4 million. The mayor’s press office says the number of police vacancies that would be eliminated in the mayor's proposed budget is 368. Another 132 sworn vacancies will become civilian positions. </p><p>The Chicago Police Department's annual budget would rise from $2.12 billion this year to $2.24 billion in 2027 to cover police pay raises.</p><p></p><p>Johnson said there is a "freeze on the number of positions, so our budget can be balanced." But it "doesn’t prevent the department from hiring as we have looked at what’s necessary, particularly through attrition." </p><p>"What they’ve requested, we’ve been able to meet. That also includes the ability for promotions as well.” </p><p> Johnson also eyes the $75 million up-front payment from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/chicago-parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-city-council-compromise-explainer" >Stonepeak Partners</a> tied to the New York investment firm’s $2.5 billion acquisition of Chicago parking meters as a way to defray the cost of the $364 million advance pension payment in 2027.</p><p>Former Finance Chair Scott Waguespack, one of the Council leaders who negotiated the deal, said he assumed that the $75 million would be over and above the pension advance, and that the ongoing profit sharing payments from Stonepeak would also be used exclusively to chip away at the city’s $36 billion pension crisis.</p><p>“Just like the head tax, we’ll reject that,” Waguespack said.</p><p>The Sports Betting Alliance, which represents DraftKings, FanDuel and other sportsbooks, is also lining up to oppose the mayor’s plan to nearly double the Chicago tax on sports betting. Johnson has argued that the $37 million in increased revenue would be “generated from the companies — not actual bettors.” But sportsbooks that have a pending lawsuit against the city said the tax burden would fall on the backs of sports fans.</p><p>“Doubling the tax rate for legal sports betting will raise the cost to play for Chicago fans and drive them out of state-licensed sportsbooks that protect consumers,” the alliance's statement said.</p>

entries.title: Bears expect to have RG Jonah Jackson vs. Patriots, rule out RB Kyle Monangai
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will have starting right guard Jonah Jackson against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/20/scandal-early-season-struggles-behind-him-mike-vrabel-has-the-patriots-back-on-track-for-super-bowl-run" >the Patriots</a> on Thursday after all. Despite leaving the Falcons game with a hip injury and the team casting doubt on the possibility early in the week, he was full-go on the final injury report Wednesday.</p><p>Jackson has been one of the Bears’ most reliable offensive linemen over the last two seasons and hasn’t missed a start.</p><p>They will, however, be missing No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai for the third consecutive game. He injured his thumb and toe while taking 30 carries in the win over the Jets on Oct. 4, and will get nearly a month off before potentially returning for the Seahawks game Nov. 2.</p><p>The Bears also ruled out backup linebacker Jack Sanborn with a concussion, listed starting linebacker T.J. Edwards as doubtful as he works back from a hamstring injury and designated cornerback Tyrique Stevenson questionable with a hamstring injury. Stevenson has fought through injuries most of the season, and the Bears projected him as a full participant all week.</p><p>The team didn’t practice due to the quick turnaround, opting for walk-throughs each day. That means any practiced participation was estimated.</p><p>The Patriots ruled out five players, including three starters: right guard Ben Brown (knee), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and cornerback Carlton Davis (neck).</p><p>Safety Kevin Byard (chest) is questionable, and star wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle) will play.</p>

entries.title: Months after storm, Gary residents are plagued with blackouts
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was originally published in </i><a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/gary-intermittent-power-outages-nipsco/" target="_blank" ><i>Capital B Gary</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>After some Gary residents endured two to three weeks without electricity in August, many are still living with uncertainty.</p><p>Residents contacted by Capital B report experiencing intermittent power disruptions even after power was restored to the city following the storm. They said they fear their lights will flicker and go dark during rains or high winds. They worry their refrigerators will go silent for several hours, sometimes even days, and food will spoil.</p><p>Residents say there were occasional power outages before the Aug. 11 storm. But the hardship of enduring a weekslong blackout has made recent interruptions even more unbearable.</p><p>Capital B Gary has reached out to NIPSCO for a statement about the intermittent blackouts, but has yet to receive a response.</p><p>Resident Sherry Smith remembers the August storm as if it were yesterday. The former Gary Common Council employee was without power for two weeks after the storm, and she said the recurring blackouts constantly keep her on edge that she’ll be plunged into darkness again.</p><p>“We need to take this seriously because we’re still having power out,” she said.</p><p>“Every time it rains, I’m thinking that my power may go out,” Smith said. “Those trees may fall on the wires, and my neighbors’ electricity will go out again.”</p><p>She’s not alone.</p><p>Westside resident and business owner Marsha Jones says her power goes out whenever it rains. After the storm struck, her lights remained dark for 19 days, water damaged her basement, and her roof leaks from two holes.</p><p>“It’s something that I never had to deal with before,” she said.</p><p>Jones hasn’t slept in her house in more than two months. Instead, she has been staying with her mother, who hasn’t experienced any other blackouts. Luckily, her business, MJ’s Boutique, avoided damage from the Aug. 11 storm and hasn’t experienced disruptions since power was restored. But she misses sleeping in her own bed.</p><p>“I want to go home,” she said. “I just want to go back to how life was before the storm.”</p><p>Jones’ frustrations are compounded by the impact on her checkbook. Her utility bill is twice what she expected to pay after almost three weeks without power. She said she spoke with NIPSCO and was told someone would come out to check her meter to see why the bill was so high.</p><p>She said she’s still waiting.</p><p>“They need to be held accountable,” Jones said. “I’m just praying for us to get back to normal.”</p><h3>Persistent power outages</h3><p>Gary Councilman Myles Tolliver Sr., who lives in Miller, said the problem predates the storm: Power interruptions have become the norm.</p><p>“The wind blows the wrong way, we lose power,” said Tolliver, whose electricity has been interrupted four times since the storm. “We might lose power for six to seven hours if the wind blows, and if it rains, we might lose power for a day or so.”</p><p>Tolliver has lost power while preparing for council meetings or while his kids do their homework. Sometimes the lights are not restored until later in the evening. Like the others, he called NIPSCO to inquire about the situation but got no explanation, only an estimated restoration time.</p><p>The utility’s failure to properly maintain power lines may be causing the problem, Tolliver said.</p><p>“If you go and just ride around the Miller area, or really Gary as a whole … you can see that the lines are embedded in tree limbs and leaves,” Tolliver said. “There are trees that were marked to be cut years ago that haven’t been cut. No maintenance has been happening.”</p><p>While he’s seen some work done, he said more is needed so Gary residents don’t have to deal with these problems, especially after storms.</p><p>After the storm, Tolliver’s house was without electricity for two and a half weeks. Without a working refrigerator, his family lost all their food.</p><p>Tolliver sent his family to a hotel outside Chicago. While they were away, he spent much of his time assisting residents in the community.</p><p>“It was some things that I don’t know if I’ll ever see again, but it was definitely life-changing,” he said. “I had to be there because they’re depending on me. It’s the reason why I’m in office to serve and make sure they get what they need.”</p><h3>Shopping differently for food</h3><p>As Gary residents struggle to recover, the memory of the lengthy power outage, combined with untimely interruptions in electric service since then, has changed how they live.</p><p>“I think everybody’s feeling that way, and I think it’s changed the trajectory of how we save food,” Tolliver said.</p><p>With nearly 40% of Gary residents receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, the community faces another layer of uncertainty.</p><p>“When I look at things differently now, I never save food as I used to,” Tolliver added. “Now it’s only buying enough to last a certain amount of time. But with food costs rising constantly and the approaching holiday/winter season, it’s hard to find a middle ground as circumstances change.”</p><p>The persistent outages led him, and many others in the Gary community, to push state officials for answers. In September, a <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/nipsco-statehouse-committee-hearing/" target="_blank" >joint committee</a> hearing at the Indiana Statehouse examined NIPSCO’s storm preparedness and response. There, Tolliver joined fellow leaders and residents in expressing frustration with the utility’s handling of the disaster.</p><p>“I think for a lot of time, elected officials tiptoe around things, and that’s one thing that I’m not going to do: I’m going to speak my truth,” Tolliver said.</p><p>Smith woke up around 4 a.m. to drive almost three hours from Gary to the Statehouse in Indianapolis to tell lawmakers about the frequent power outages.</p><p>“This happened before the derecho. It happened during the derecho, and it’s still happening as we get ready to come into the winter months,” she said while speaking on the House floor.</p><p>The weekend before her testimony, Smith said, her power went out around 11:30 a.m. Saturday and returned around 4 p.m. The following day, it went out again between 1:30 a.m. and 4 a.m.</p><p>“It wasn’t any type of storm or anything,” she recalled. “It was a nice day, and the power just went out.”</p>

entries.title: 2nd woman alleging sexual assault at a University of Chicago frat house feared she was drugged: police report
entries.summary: <p>A woman told Chicago police she feared she was drugged before being sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago fraternity house earlier this year, according to a police report.</p><p>On Feb. 8, a day after the assault reportedly happened, the 19-year-old told officers the alleged assailant gave her a shot of alcohol that “might have been laced,” the report says.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >The woman filed a lawsuit</a> Monday against the local and national Alpha Delta Phi organizations, alleging a member of the fraternity had assaulted “her limp body” during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi house, 5747 S. University Ave. The woman was identified only as “Jane Doe.”</p><p>The lawsuit came soon after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >another woman reported she was sexually assaulted</a> on Oct. 11 at an off-campus party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house, located just a block away at 5625 S. University Ave. Witnesses in that case reported the accuser appeared “significantly more intoxicated than expected based on her reported alcohol consumption," according to another police report.</p><p>The two cases have placed the University of Chicago at the center of a national reckoning over sexual violence at colleges, sparked by reports of gang rape and drugging at a fraternity house at Cornell University in upstate New York.</p><p>The University of Chicago previously alerted students to <a class="Link" href="https://safety-security.uchicago.edu/News-Alerts/2022-11-03-Security-and-Safety-Notice" target="_blank" >a spate of alleged druggings</a> in November 2022, warning of seven reports of undergraduates who suspected their drinks had been spiked at parties.</p><p>In one case, a student reported they were “likely sexually assaulted.” The university said at the time that “such behavior is unacceptable, not tolerated within this community, and may be criminal.”</p><p>Elizabeth Spratt, former toxicology director for Westchester County in New York, said “timing is everything” when it comes to testing for potential drugs, noting levels could be low by the following morning. "These [cases] break my heart, because they're ... hard to prove because of timing," Spratt said.</p><p>The women alleging they were assaulted at the two fraternity houses aren’t students at the University of Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-dd0000" name="html-embed-module-dd0000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The woman identified in her lawsuit as Jane Doe said she had two shots of alcohol at the Alpha Delta Phi house before meeting the alleged assailant, according to the police report. The suspect, identified in the lawsuit and the report as Kevin Shim, then gave Jane Doe another shot, after which she told police she “vaguely remembers anything,” the report says.</p><p>In the lawsuit, she said she felt “unsteady and lightheaded” almost immediately after taking the drink. She was then brought to an upstairs bedroom where the fraternity member assaulted her and left her “alone and unconscious,” according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Other fraternity members blocked her friends from getting to the bedroom as the assault was happening, the lawsuit says.</p><p>Jane Doe went to Chicago police the next morning and was treated at Illinois Masonic Hospital, according to the lawsuit and the report.</p><p>The lawsuit doesn’t mention she was potentially drugged, but her lawyer continued to raise that allegation in an interview.</p><p>“This situation is someone that really took all the right steps,” Georgia Booth, one of Jane Doe’s attorneys, said in an interview. “The next morning, she went to the hospital, got a toxicology report and a rape kit done, and then immediately spoke to the Chicago Police Department.”</p><p>But months later, the police investigation is still pending. Booth said she’s requested additional information but has only been provided the original incident report — and not the findings of the toxicology or sexual assault testing.</p><p>Booth said she had “no idea” why there still weren’t any charges in the case.</p><p>“Unfortunately, I work with survivors of sexual assaults primarily in my practice,” Booth said. “I work with clients that have made similar reports to the Chicago Police Department. Sometimes they get little to no investigation done into their experience. So we're encouraging the police department to continue investigating, and hopefully charges will be brought soon.”</p><p>The university, the police department and the national Alpha Delta Phi organization didn’t respond to questions Wednesday.</p><p>The university previously said the allegations in the lawsuit were “disturbing.”</p><p>“The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault,” the spokesperson said in a statement Tuesday. “The University is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the fraternity. The University will cooperate by providing information and is prepared to help the Chicago Police Department in its investigation.”</p><p>Alpha Delta Phi said "the member involved" was suspended from the fraternity after the organization became aware of the reported assault, which it takes “extremely seriously.” Shim hasn't responded to a request for comment.</p><p>The university will hold a public safety meeting Wednesday evening. The agenda was set in September but includes discussions of “sexual misconduct protocols and support systems, along with other public safety topics,” a university spokesperson said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >Group cheered as woman was sexually assaulted at University of Chicago frat house, police report says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/14/university-of-chicago-sexual" >No arrests in wake of reported sexual assault at University of Chicago frat house, police say</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >Another woman says she was sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago fraternity party</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
